title: Computers & the Internet: The Big Picture
objective: After this level you can follow a single photo from your phone's switches and software, across the internet, to a friend's screen.
summary: One photo, start to finish: the camera turns light into binary numbers, switches follow software, packets cross a network of networks, and pixels rebuild it.

cards.headline: Tap send. A photo leaves your phone and lands on a friend's.
cards.body: Between your tap and their screen, the photo becomes numbers, gets handled by billions of tiny switches, is broken into pieces and is rebuilt on the other side. This level follows that one photo the whole way. The rest of the tree zooms in on each stop.

cards.headline: Stop 1: light becomes numbers
cards.body: Your camera's sensor is covered in light receptors called pixels. Light hitting each one makes a tiny electric current, and the phone translates that into binary digits, 0s and 1s, for storage. From that moment your photo isn't a picture in any ordinary sense. It's a very long list of numbers, which is exactly what a computer can store and move.

mascot.line: Keep this map in mind. Every chapter ahead zooms in on one stop of this trip.

cards.headline: Stop 2: switches that follow orders
cards.body: Inside the phone, the processor holds billions of transistors, tiny switches that open and close on every tick of its clock. The switches have no idea what a photo is. Software does the telling: an app is a set of instructions that tells the hardware what to do with those numbers. Hardware does the work; software gives the orders.

cards.headline: Stop 3: in pieces across the internet
cards.body: The internet is a network of networks, with routers linking them. Your photo doesn't cross it in one piece. It's broken into small packets that each travel on their own, by whatever route is available, and your friend's phone reassembles them. Then it turns the numbers back into a grid of pixels, each a mix of red, green and blue light. Numbers in, numbers out, and a beach in between.

title: A Bit: The Smallest Fact
objective: After this level you can explain a bit as one yes-or-no choice and why eight bits make a byte with 256 possible patterns.
summary: A bit is one choice between two options, 1 or 0, stored by a switch. Each added bit doubles the patterns, so a byte of 8 bits has 256.

cards.headline: The smallest fact a computer can hold is a yes or a no.
cards.body: Is the light on? Is the answer yes? One question, two possible answers. Computers build everything, your photos included, out of answers that small. So how does something so tiny add up to so much?

cards.headline: One choice, one bit
cards.body: A bit, short for binary digit, holds the answer to one choice between two options, written 1 or 0. Inside a chip, a transistor switch stores it: on is 1, off is 0. John Tukey is credited with first using the word, in a 1947 memo, and Claude Shannon's 1948 paper was the first to put it in print. Fittingly, the word is itself a small bit of a longer phrase.

cards.headline: Every bit doubles your options
cards.body: One bit gives 2 patterns: 0 or 1. Add a second and you get 4: 00, 01, 10 and 11. A third makes 8. Each extra bit doubles the count, because every old pattern can now end in either a 0 or a 1. It's the same reason a guessing game of yes-or-no questions narrows things down so fast.

cards.fact: Eight bits make a byte: 256 possible patterns.
cards.context: Start with 2 and keep doubling: 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256. That's eight bits, and a group of eight is called a byte. One byte can take any of 256 different patterns, from all 0s to all 1s. That is a surprising amount of room for eight tiny switches.

title: Kilobytes to Terabytes
objective: After this level you can compare the sizes of a text message, a photo, a movie and a whole drive in bytes.
summary: Kilo, mega, giga and tera each mean 1,000 times more bytes: a text is dozens, a photo megabytes, an HD film gigabytes. A 1 TB drive shows as 931 GB in Windows.

cards.headline: A text message and a hard drive are measured in the same thing.
cards.body: Bytes, from Level 2: eight bits each. The only difference is how many. Kilo, mega, giga and tera are the counting words, and the jumps between them are bigger than they sound.

cards.headline: Every step is a thousand times bigger
cards.body: Storage borrows the metric prefixes: kilo means a thousand, mega a million, giga a billion and tera a trillion. So a kilobyte is about 1,000 bytes, and each step up is 1,000 times the last. A typed character takes about one byte, so a short text of a few dozen characters is a few dozen bytes. A single megabyte could hold thousands of them.

title: How Letters Become Numbers
objective: After this level you can explain how codes like ASCII and Unicode give every letter, symbol and emoji its own number.
summary: ASCII (1963) gave 128 characters 7-bit numbers, A is 65. Unicode gives every character in every script a unique number, emoji included.

cards.headline: Type A. Your computer stores 65.
cards.body: There is no letter shape inside the machine, only numbers. In the standard code, uppercase A is 65 and B is 66. So who decided, and how did every computer come to agree?

cards.headline: ASCII: one codebook, 128 characters
cards.body: ASCII, approved as an American standard in 1963, gives letters, digits and punctuation marks standard numbers. It uses 7-bit codes, which by Level 2's doubling makes 128 patterns, so 128 characters. One neat detail: uppercase P is 1010000 and lowercase p is 1110000. The two differ in a single bit. Capital or small, one switch apart.

cards.headline: Too many codebooks, then one
cards.body: 128 characters could never cover the world's writing. For years, hundreds of rival encodings filled the gap, and they clashed: two could use the same number for two different characters. Unicode fixed that by giving every character a unique number, whatever the platform, program or language. Unicode 18.0, released in September 2026, holds 172,808 characters. It kept ASCII's numbers, too: its UTF-8 form is backward-compatible.

cards.headline: An emoji is a number too
cards.body: Send a laughing face and you're really sending a number. The Unicode Consortium standardizes emoji codes, and your friend's phone receives the number and draws its own picture for it. That's why the same emoji can look a little different on another maker's phone. You chose the number. Their phone chose the drawing.

title: Pictures and Sound as Numbers
objective: After this level you can explain how a photo becomes a grid of pixel numbers and a song becomes thousands of samples a second.
summary: A photo is a grid of pixels, each three numbers from 0 to 255 for red, green and blue. A song is samples: a CD measures the wave 44,100 times a second.

cards.headline: A photo is a grid. A song is a queue.
cards.body: Level 1 said your photo becomes numbers. But which numbers? And sound flows through time, so how does it turn into a list? Two tricks: cut space into tiny squares, and cut time into tiny slices.

cards.headline: Pixels: squares made of three numbers
cards.body: Zoom far enough into a digital photo and you reach pixels: small squares, each one color, laid out in a grid. Each pixel's color is a mix of red, green and blue light, and each of the three gets a number from 0, off, to 255, full brightness. That fits in one byte per color, so three bytes paint one pixel.

cards.fact: Three bytes per pixel allow 16,777,216 colors.
cards.context: Red, green and blue each have 256 settings, so the possible mixes number 256 × 256 × 256, or 16,777,216. Every shade in your photo is one pick from that list. Three small numbers, more than sixteen million possibilities.

cards.headline: Sound: measure, measure, measure
cards.body: To record sound digitally, a device measures the sound wave at points spaced evenly in time and writes each measurement down as a binary number, called a sample. A CD takes 44,100 samples every second. Why so many? To capture a sound you must sample more than twice as fast as its highest frequency, and human hearing reaches about 20 kHz. So CDs needed more than about 40,000 a second.

title: Logic Gates: AND, OR, NOT
objective: After this level you can explain how AND, OR and NOT gates turn yes-or-no inputs into a yes-or-no output.
summary: Logic gates turn yes-or-no inputs into one output: AND needs all 1s, OR any 1, NOT flips. Boole wrote the algebra; Shannon showed switches could do it.

cards.headline: A lamp with two switches can already do logic.
cards.body: Wire a lamp so it lights only when both of two switches are closed. That lamp is answering a question: is switch A on, and is switch B on? Computers are built from tiny deciders just like it.

cards.headline: Gates are switches in disguise
cards.body: A logic gate takes yes-or-no inputs, 1s and 0s, and produces one yes-or-no output. It works like a switch, passing or blocking electrical pulses, and its circuits are built from parts such as transistors, the same on-off switches that store Level 2's bits. Wire gates together and they can even do arithmetic. That's the next level's trick.

cards.headline: The math came first
cards.body: In 1847 and 1854 George Boole worked out an algebra of logic, now called Boolean algebra, in which statements are simply true or false, written 1 or 0. Much later, Claude Shannon's master's thesis used Boolean algebra to lay the theoretical groundwork for digital circuits. In other words, circuits full of switches could be worked out with algebra, on paper.

title: Adding With Switches
objective: After this level you can explain how a handful of logic gates can add two binary numbers, the first step toward all computing.
summary: In binary 1 + 1 = 10: write 0, carry 1. An exclusive-OR makes the sum and an AND the carry; chained full adders add numbers of any length.

cards.headline: Your phone adds numbers, yet none of its gates knows what a number is.
cards.body: Level 6's gates only answer yes or no. Wire a few of them together, though, and they add two bits. The trick is noticing that adding in binary is itself a yes-or-no puzzle.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the circuit. Remember the idea: 1 + 1 means write 0, carry 1.

cards.headline: Adding with only 0 and 1
cards.body: Adding two bits has just four cases: 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 0 = 1, and 1 + 1 = 10. That last one is binary for two: write 0 and carry 1 to the next place, like carrying in 9 + 1. So 3 + 1, written 11 + 01 in binary, carries twice and lands on 100, which is 4.

cards.headline: Two gates make a half adder
cards.body: Look at the four cases again. The sum digit is 1 when exactly one input is 1. That's called exclusive OR, and it can be built from Level 6's AND, OR and NOT. The carry is 1 only when both inputs are 1: plain AND. Put an exclusive-OR and an AND side by side and you have a half adder, a circuit that adds two bits.

cards.headline: Chain them to add anything
cards.body: A half adder ignores any carry coming in. A full adder adds three bits: two digits plus the carry from the place to its right. Line full adders up, each one's carry feeding the next, and you can add long binary numbers. Wired-up gates like these do the arithmetic in a processor's arithmetic-logic unit, which adds, subtracts, multiplies, divides and compares.

title: The Processor's Endless Loop
objective: After this level you can explain the fetch, decode and execute cycle a processor repeats billions of times a second.
summary: A processor fetches the instruction its program counter points to, decodes it, executes it and repeats, paced by a clock ticking billions of times a second.

cards.headline: Your processor knows one routine. It runs it billions of times a second.
cards.body: Every app, game and photo filter comes down to the same three steps, repeated without a break: get an instruction, work out what it means, do it. This is the loop at the heart of the machine.

cards.headline: Fetch, decode, execute
cards.body: The processor keeps a program counter: the memory address of the next instruction. Fetch: it collects the instruction stored at that address. Decode: it splits the instruction's binary pattern into parts, each with a meaning, such as 'add' and which numbers to add. Execute: it carries out the operation, perhaps sending two numbers through Level 7's adders.

cards.headline: Then again, and again
cards.body: After each fetch, the program counter usually steps on to the next instruction, so the processor works through a program in order. Some instructions, called jumps and branches, change the counter to point somewhere else, which lets a program go back and repeat or skip ahead. When one instruction is done, the cycle simply starts over.

cards.fact: A 3.2 GHz processor runs 3.2 billion clock cycles every second.
cards.context: A clock sends out pulses at a fixed, precise rate, and those pulses keep the fetch, decode and execute steps in time. Gigahertz means billions of cycles per second. On every single cycle, billions of transistors inside the processor open and close.

title: Why Memory Comes in Layers
objective: After this level you can explain why a computer keeps data in layers, from tiny fast cache to roomy RAM to big slow storage.
summary: Main memory is far slower than the processor, so memory comes in layers: registers and SRAM cache on the chip, denser DRAM main memory, then cheap storage.

cards.headline: Your processor is faster than its own memory.
cards.body: A processor can do a sum in a nanosecond or less. Fetching a number from main memory typically takes 20 to 80 nanoseconds. Level 8's loop fetches all the time, so without a plan the fastest part of the computer would spend most of its time waiting.

cards.headline: Why not make it all fast?
cards.body: Because fast memory costs space and money. Cache is made of SRAM, which is quick but physically large: a chip the same size holds several times as much of the slower DRAM used for main memory. So memory comes as a hierarchy, from fast, expensive registers inside the processor down to slower, cheaper storage. Think of a desk, a bookshelf and a warehouse.

mascot.line: This connects to Level 8: every fetch asks memory for something. Cache keeps many of those trips short.

cards.headline: Why a small cache is enough
cards.body: Programs are creatures of habit. They repeat the same instructions in loops and work on related data, a pattern called locality of reference. So once values are copied from main memory into the cache, many later requests find them already there. A cache of up to several megabytes near the processor takes a lot of the waiting out of the loop.

Gates built from switches combine bits, and adders built from gates do sums. title: Punched Cards
objective: After this level you can explain how punched cards steered a weaving loom in 1804 and counted the 1890 US census.
summary: Jacquard's 1804 loom read punched cards, a hole lifting a thread and no hole leaving it down. Hollerith's pins, holes and mercury counted the 1890 census in six months.

cards.headline: Long before screens, machines took orders from holes in cards.
cards.body: A French loom wove patterns by reading punched cards. Decades later, an American census was counted with them, as pins dropped through holes and closed electric circuits. Two very different jobs, one simple trick. What can a hole tell a machine?

cards.headline: A loom that reads
cards.body: In 1804 Joseph-Marie Jacquard patented a loom steered by a chain of interchangeable punched cards. Pins pressed against each card in turn. Where a pin found a hole, it passed through, and its hook raised a warp thread. Where it met solid card, it was stopped, and that thread stayed down. Swap the cards and the same loom wove a different pattern, automatically.

cards.headline: A hole is a yes or a no
cards.body: Look at one spot on a card. Either it has a hole or it doesn't, and the loom does one of two things: lift the thread or leave it. That is one choice between two options, exactly what Level 2 called a bit. A whole card is just a row of those choices, set out in advance.

cards.fact: Tabulating the 1880 US census by hand dragged on until 1887.
cards.context: Herman Hollerith's answer was a machine that read one punched card per person. Metal pins dropped onto the card. Where a pin passed through a hole, it dipped into mercury, closing an electric circuit that nudged a counting dial forward. With his machines, the 1890 population count took six months, ahead of schedule and under budget.

cards.headline: From census cards to IBM
cards.body: Hollerith's company, the Tabulating Machine Company, went through a series of mergers. In 1924 it took a new name: International Business Machines, or IBM. The company began by counting holes in cards.

title: Ada Lovelace's Big Idea
objective: After this level you can explain Lovelace's 1843 insight that Babbage's Analytical Engine could work with symbols, not just numbers.
summary: Babbage's Analytical Engine, never built, was to read punched cards and hold a store and a mill. Lovelace's 1843 notes saw it might act on things besides number, such as music.

cards.headline: A machine built for sums, and a woman who saw it could do more.
cards.body: Charles Babbage designed an engine to calculate. In 1843 Ada Lovelace published notes on it that asked a bigger question: if a machine can work with numbers, what else could those numbers stand for?

cards.headline: An engine run by cards
cards.body: In the 1830s Babbage conceived the Analytical Engine, a general-purpose calculating machine to be programmed with punched cards, the very trick Jacquard's loom used for its patterns. The design had a store to hold numbers and a separate mill to do the arithmetic. Think of them as memory and processor. The funding never came, and it was never built.

cards.fact: In 1843 Lovelace published notes on the Analytical Engine.
cards.context: She had translated an article about the engine by the Italian mathematician Luigi Menabrea, then added extensive notes of her own. In them she compared the engine to the loom: it would weave algebraic patterns just as the Jacquard loom weaves flowers and leaves.

cards.headline: Numbers that stand for other things
cards.body: Her boldest line: the engine "might act upon other things besides number." If the rules of harmony could be written in its terms, she suggested, it might even compose elaborate pieces of music. The key is that a number doesn't have to be a quantity. It can stand for a letter, a symbol or a musical note, and a machine can work on those too.

title: Turing's Imaginary Machine
objective: After this level you can explain Alan Turing's 1936 idea of a simple machine reading a tape, and why it can compute anything computable.
summary: Turing's 1936 machine: a tape of squares, a head that reads, writes and moves one square at a time, and a finite rulebook. A universal machine runs any machine's rules from its tape.

cards.headline: In 1936 Alan Turing described a computer made of little more than a tape.
cards.body: It was an abstract machine, an idea on paper rather than a device to build. So why does a machine that never existed sit at the heart of computer science?

cards.headline: A tape, a head and a rulebook
cards.body: Picture a tape divided into squares, as long as you need, each blank or holding one symbol. A head sits over one square at a time. It can read the symbol there, write or erase one, and move one square left or right. At every moment the machine is in one of a limited number of states, and a finite table of instructions says what to do next. That's the whole machine.

mascot.line: Keep this: a program can be written down as data for another machine to read. Every computer since builds on that.

cards.headline: One machine that can be any machine
cards.body: Turing's cleverest step was to write a machine's instructions onto the tape itself. His universal machine reads that description and then does whatever the described machine would do. Change what's on the tape, and the same machine does a different job.

cards.fact: Everything humanly computable can be computed by a universal Turing machine.
cards.context: That claim is called the Church-Turing thesis. Strictly, it can't be proved, because it matches an everyday idea, what can be computed, to a precise definition. It's a thesis, not a theorem.

title: ENIAC and Its Programmers
objective: After this level you can explain how ENIAC was programmed by rewiring cables and switches, and who did that work.
summary: ENIAC was programmed by hand, connecting wires and setting switches for days per problem. Six women, former human computers, worked out how from its diagrams, uncredited for decades.

cards.headline: ENIAC's first programmers had no manuals and no programming languages.
cards.body: ENIAC was built from 1943 to 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania. Making it solve a problem meant working out, by hand, how to wire it. Six women did that work, and the photos and articles that followed featured only men.

cards.headline: Programming with cables
cards.body: Turing's universal machine read its instructions from a tape. ENIAC's lived in its wiring. To set it up for a new problem, people worked out a configuration, then connected wires between its panels and set its switches by hand. That took many days. Once its plugboards were set, though, ENIAC ran at electronic speed.

cards.headline: The six
cards.body: Kathleen McNulty, Jean Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Frances Bilas and Ruth Lichterman had worked as human computers, calculating trajectories for the US Army. Now they were handed ENIAC's wiring and logical diagrams, with no manuals and no programming languages, and they worked out how its panels fit together. They were learning to program a machine nobody had programmed before.

cards.fact: Jennings and Snyder devised the program for ENIAC's February 1946 debut.
cards.context: It calculated a trajectory. Yet the women weren't invited to the celebration dinner that followed. Recognition came much later: in 1997 all six were inducted into the Women in Technology International Hall of Fame.

title: Keeping the Program in Memory
objective: After this level you can explain why storing the program in memory beside its data, first done in 1948, made computers flexible.
summary: A stored-program computer keeps instructions in memory beside its data, proposed in 1945, so a program changes without rewiring. The Manchester Baby first did it on June 21, 1948.

cards.headline: What if changing a program meant changing numbers, not cables?
cards.body: Setting ENIAC up for each problem took many days of wiring and switch setting. The fix sounds almost too simple: keep the instructions in the computer's memory, right beside the data they work on.

mascot.line: This is Level 13's universal machine made real: the program is just more data for the machine to read.

cards.headline: Instructions are data too
cards.body: In a stored-program computer, instructions and data sit together in the same memory. John von Neumann and colleagues proposed the design in 1945, for a machine called EDVAC. Because a program is just more data in memory, it can be changed, moved or even produced by another program, with no rewiring at all.

cards.fact: On June 21, 1948, the Manchester Baby ran a program stored in its memory.
cards.context: It was the first computer to do so. Frederic Williams, Tom Kilburn and Geoff Tootill built it at the University of Manchester. Its memory was a Williams-Kilburn tube, which stored bits on a cathode-ray tube. Its first program searched for the highest factor of a number, not glamorous, but it worked.

cards.headline: The birth of software
cards.body: The Computer History Museum calls this moment the birth of software: storing a computer's instructions in its memory, as every computer since has done. A new job now meant loading new instructions, not days with cables and switches.

title: The Transistor
objective: After this level you can explain how the 1947 transistor replaced hot, fragile vacuum tubes as the computer's switch.
summary: Vacuum tubes switched with heated cathodes that used power and burned out. In 1947 Bardeen and Brattain made the transistor at Bell Labs: a small, cool, reliable switch that replaced tubes.

cards.headline: ENIAC lost one of its vacuum tubes roughly every day or two.
cards.body: It had about 18,000 of them, and each one was a switch that could fail. Computing needed a switch that didn't run hot and burn out.

cards.headline: A switch that's also a heater
cards.body: A vacuum tube controls a stream of electrons. To get those electrons, its cathode is heated to about 1,000°C or more, which takes significant power and gives off a lot of heat. And like an old light bulb, tubes tend to burn out, mainly when their heated filaments fail.

cards.headline: Three physicists at Bell Labs
cards.body: In December 1947 at Bell Labs, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain made the first working transistor, from a small piece of germanium. They worked in a solid-state physics group organized by William Shockley. In 1956 the three shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for their discovery of the transistor effect. A team effort, not a lone genius.

cards.fact: Transistors are small, run cool, are highly reliable and use little power.
cards.context: A transistor can work as a switch: if current flows, the circuit is on, and if not, it's off. That's the on-off switch that stores Level 2's bits. By the late 1950s transistors had replaced vacuum tubes in many uses, and complex circuits could shrink.

title: Chips and Moore's Law

summary: Wiring separate parts held circuits back until the integrated circuit (Kilby 1958, Noyce 1959) built parts and connections on one piece of silicon. Moore's 1965 forecast became a target.

cards.headline: The hardest part of early electronics wasn't the parts. It was the wires.
cards.body: Transistors were small, but as electronic systems grew, thousands of them had to be wired to each other and to other parts. That wiring became the main obstacle to making circuits smaller.

cards.headline: Everything on one piece
cards.body: An integrated circuit, or chip, builds transistors, other components and the connections between them on one thin piece of semiconductor, usually silicon. Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments in 1958 and Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor in 1959 each developed it independently, and both are credited. Noyce's version laid metal connections on top of the silicon, doing away with loose wires between parts. The wiring comes built in.

mascot.line: Don't memorize 65,000. Remember the shape: double, then double again.

cards.fact: In 1965 Gordon Moore predicted chips would double their components every year.
cards.context: Writing in Electronics magazine, he projected about 65,000 components on a chip by 1975. In 1975, as growth began to slow, he revised the pace to a doubling every two years.

cards.headline: A forecast, not physics
cards.body: Nothing in nature forces chips to double. Moore's law is an observation about an industry, not a law of physics. Meeting Moore's timetable became a goal for engineers, and chasing it helped make it come true.

title: The Computer Comes Home
objective: After this level you can explain how the cheap microprocessor led to the Altair, the Apple II and the IBM PC, and put computers in homes.
summary: A processor on one chip (the 4004, 1971) made personal computers affordable: the 1975 Altair kit of switches and lights, the ready-made 1977 machines, then the 1981 IBM PC standard.

cards.headline: In 1971, a whole processor fit on one chip.
cards.body: Intel's 4004, the first microprocessor, put a complete general-purpose processor on a single chip with 2,300 transistors. A powerful processor on one chip is what made affordable personal computers possible. Here's how the computer came home.

cards.headline: A kit with switches for a keyboard
cards.body: In January 1975 the magazine Popular Electronics ran a cover story on the Altair 8800, a computer kit from a company called MITS, built around Intel's 8080 microprocessor. cards.body: In 1977 three preassembled, mass-produced personal computers arrived: the Apple II, the Commodore PET and the TRS-80. The Apple II was sold complete, with a keyboard, case and power supply. No kit to assemble.

cards.fact: The IBM PC, unveiled in August 1981, set the industry standard.
cards.context: It used Intel's 8088 processor and an operating system from Microsoft, later called MS-DOS. IBM built it from off-the-shelf parts and published a technical reference. Other companies built their own IBM-compatible computers with Intel processors and MS-DOS, and the design became an industry standard.

title: Spell Out Every Step
objective: After this level you can explain why a program must spell out every step exactly, because a computer never fills in what you meant.
summary: A computer is powerful but literal: every step must be defined for every case, as Knuth's test of definiteness says, or a units mix-up can lose a spacecraft at Mars.

cards.headline: In 1999, a spacecraft was lost at Mars over one unspoken word: the unit.
cards.body: Two pieces of Mars Climate Orbiter's ground software each assumed a different system of units. Neither program could notice the other's assumption. To see why not, start with what a computer really does with your instructions.

cards.headline: Powerful, and completely literal
cards.body: Stanford's CS101 course sums up a computer as "Powerful + Stupid". It can run billions of operations a second, but each one is simple and mechanical, like adding or comparing two numbers. There is no insight in there, no sense of what you meant. So a person has to break every task into steps that small and spell them out. The computer brings the speed; you bring the understanding.

mascot.line: Keep this: a step a person would understand isn't enough. For a computer, it has to leave nothing to guess.

cards.headline: A recipe isn't a program
cards.body: The computer scientist Donald Knuth set a test for any algorithm, called definiteness: every step must be precisely defined, with its action spelled out for each case. Recipes fail it. "Add a dash of salt" works for a cook, but how much is a dash, and where does it go? That's why programs are written in formal languages where every statement has one definite meaning, and why code must follow its rules exactly or it won't run at all.

cards.headline: What the orbiter was never told
cards.body: One piece of Mars Climate Orbiter's ground software reported thruster data in English units, while the navigation software that used it expected metric, and nothing translated between them. The mismatched numbers threw off the trajectory calculations and sent the spacecraft too close to Mars. The last contact came on 23 September 1999; it burned up in the planet's atmosphere. Each program followed its steps faithfully. No step said which unit.

title: From Code to Machine Code
objective: After this level you can explain how compilers and interpreters turn code people can read into instructions a processor runs.
summary: Only machine code runs on a processor, and each processor family has its own. Compilers translate ahead of time; interpreters, bytecode and just-in-time compilers translate as the program runs.

cards.headline: Your processor has never read a line of code you'd recognize.
cards.body: Only machine code actually runs on a processor. Everything else, from a game to a photo filter, was written in a language people can read and then translated. You met compilers in Everyday Technology. Here's what comes out of them, and the other ways the translation happens.

cards.headline: Every processor family has its own tongue
cards.body: Machine code is a processor's native language, hardwired into the chip's design. Each family of compatible processors, such as Intel's x86, has its own machine code, and other families can't run it. The instructions are extremely simple, like adding two numbers or testing whether a number is zero, and each takes just a few bytes. A big program is millions of them.

cards.headline: Translate once, ahead of time
cards.body: A compiler translates a whole program in advance. Firefox's source code, for example, is compiled into Firefox.exe, a file made mostly of machine code bytes. No single machine instruction can print, so even one line of source code becomes many instructions. And with only the finished file, you can run the program but not change it: programmers edit the human-readable source code, then compile again.

cards.headline: Or translate as it runs
cards.body: Python is interpreted: you run the source file directly, with no separate program file to build. Its standard interpreter first compiles the code into bytecode, an in-between form that a virtual machine carries out. JavaScript in your browser takes a third road: every major browser's engine has a built-in just-in-time compiler that turns code into machine code while the page runs. Different routes, one destination.

title: Why So Many Languages?
objective: After this level you can explain why languages like Python, JavaScript and C all exist, each suited to different jobs.
summary: C was built to write Unix and stays close to the machine; JavaScript runs in every major browser; Python is quick to write but, being interpreted, generally slower. Each language is a trade-off.

cards.headline: Why isn't there just one programming language?
cards.body: Because every language is a bargain. Some make life easier for the programmer; others squeeze the most from the machine; one is simply everywhere you browse. Three famous languages show three different bargains.

cards.headline: C: close to the machine
cards.body: Dennis Ritchie turned an earlier language into C at Bell Labs between 1971 and 1973, to write the Unix operating system; in summer 1973 the Unix kernel was rewritten in it. C's types and operations mirror what real processors do, which made it efficient enough to replace assembly language for building systems. Ritchie's own verdict: "C is quirky, flawed, and an enormous success."

cards.headline: JavaScript: the language of the browser
cards.body: Brendan Eich created JavaScript while working at Netscape, and it arrived in the Netscape Navigator 2.0 browser in September 1995. Today it runs primarily in web browsers, where it changes what's on a page, fetches data from servers and draws graphics. Its great strength is reach: every major browser has a JavaScript engine built in.

cards.headline: Python: quick to write, slower to run
cards.body: Guido van Rossum started Python over the 1989 Christmas holidays and posted it publicly in February 1991. It's a high-level, general-purpose language with a large standard library, and it's interpreted. That's its bargain: interpreted languages typically have a shorter write-and-fix cycle than compiled ones, but their programs generally run more slowly. Picking a language means picking which cost you'd rather pay.

title: Remember, Choose, Repeat
objective: After this level you can explain the three moves nearly every program makes: storing values in variables, choosing with if, and repeating with loops.
summary: Variables name changing values, conditionals pick between paths, and loops repeat until a condition is met. Under the hood, ifs and loops are jumps that move the program counter.

cards.headline: Count your unread messages. You just ran a tiny program.
cards.body: You kept a running total, checked each message, and repeated until there were none left. Remembering a value, choosing between paths and repeating steps are the basic moves programs are built from. Here's each one.

cards.headline: Remember: variables
cards.body: A variable is a name that refers to a value, so a value you can't predict can still be reached by a name you picked in advance. Call it unread. It starts at zero, and every time the program finds an unread message, it adds one to whatever unread holds right now. The name never changes; the value inside it does. That's the whole idea of a variable.

cards.headline: Choose: if
cards.body: A conditional runs some instructions only if a condition is met, and different ones if it isn't. Written out, it reads almost like English: if this message is unread, add one to unread; otherwise, move on. One test, two possible paths, and the program takes exactly one of them each time.

cards.headline: Repeat: loops, and what's underneath
cards.body: A loop repeats a set of instructions until a condition is met, like a counter reaching a set number or, here, running out of messages. Down at the level of machine code, both moves become jumps, which Level 8 showed you: a loop is an instruction that jumps back to an earlier point, and an if is one that skips over instructions when a condition is true.

title: Binary Search: Halve and Halve Again
objective: After this level you can explain how binary search finds one name in a sorted list of a million in about 20 steps.
summary: Checking a sorted list's middle and discarding half each time finds one name among a million in about 20 steps, and doubling the list adds only one more.

cards.headline: One name in a million. About 20 tries.
cards.body: Checking names one by one could take a million steps. There's a way that needs at most about 20, and it's the way you'd hunt through a phone book.

cards.headline: Open it in the middle
cards.body: Binary search starts at the middle of a sorted list and asks one question: is the name I want before this point or after it? Whichever half can't hold it gets thrown away, and the same question goes to the half that's left. Half, then half again, until one name remains. It only works if the list is sorted; in a jumbled list, the middle tells you nothing.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the 20. Remember the move: look in the middle, throw half away, repeat.

cards.headline: Why a million takes about 20
cards.body: A linear search checks items one by one, so in the worst case a million items take a million checks. Binary search halves what's left each time: a million sorted items need at most about 20 steps. Double the list to two million and it needs only about 21. The list grew by a million names; the work grew by one question.

cards.context: It's Level 2's doubling in reverse. There, each added bit doubled the number of patterns. Here, each question halves the names still in play, so twice as many names cost just one more question.

title: Why Some Recipes Scale Badly
objective: After this level you can explain how the steps an algorithm needs grow as its input grows, and why that decides whether it is usable.
summary: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's steps grow with its input. Doubling the data adds one step, doubles or quadruples the work, and brute-force route checking grows so fast it is ruled out.

cards.headline: Two recipes give the same answer. Only one finishes.

title: One Processor, Many Programs
objective: After this level you can explain how the operating system switches the processor between programs so quickly they seem to run at once.
summary: A timer hands control back to the operating system every few milliseconds, and a context switch saves one program's place and restores another's. Multicore chips truly run programs at once.

cards.headline: Music, a download and your typing, all on one processor core.
cards.body: Everyday Technology showed the trick: programs take turns in tiny slices, running one for a little while, then another. But a program never volunteers to stop. So how does the operating system take the processor back, and how does each program pick up exactly where it left off?

cards.headline: An alarm clock that can't be ignored
cards.body: At start-up, the operating system sets a hardware timer to raise an interrupt every few milliseconds. When it fires, whatever program is running is halted and the operating system's own handler runs instead. Without it, a program stuck in an endless loop could keep the processor forever, and your only fix would be to reboot. With it, the operating system always gets control back.

cards.headline: Saving your place
cards.body: Now the operating system can switch programs. This context switch is simple in principle: save the running program's registers and program counter, then restore the saved ones of the next program. The program counter matters most, because it holds the address of the next instruction the processor will fetch. So when a paused program gets its turn again, it resumes exactly where it stopped.

cards.headline: Waiting in line, and extra cores
cards.body: A program waiting on a disk can be blocked for milliseconds or longer, so the scheduler gives the processor to another program meanwhile. And most devices now have multicore chips, several processor cores on one chip, which really do run programs at the same moment. The catch: a typical program uses only one core unless it's rewritten to run in parallel.

title: Where Deleted Files Go
objective: After this level you can explain how a file system tracks where files live, and why a "deleted" file can often be recovered.
summary: A file system links names to inodes and marks blocks free or used. Deleting removes the link and marks space free without erasing it, so data often survives until overwritten; SSDs often wipe it.

cards.headline: You emptied the trash. The photo may still be on the drive.
cards.body: Deleting feels final, but on many drives it's more like crossing a name out of a library catalog while the book stays on the shelf. A deleted file is typically not erased at all. To see why, look at how a drive keeps track of files in the first place.

cards.headline: A catalog, not a pile
cards.body: Many file systems keep three kinds of records. A directory is a list of entries, each pairing a file's name with an inode number. The inode records facts about the file, including its size and where its blocks of data sit on the drive. And a bitmap tracks free space with one bit per block: 0 if the block is free, 1 if it's in use.

mascot.line: People mix these two up all the time. Deleting hides a file. Erasing destroys the data.

cards.headline: What delete really does
cards.body: Deleting removes the link between a file's name and its inode. Once no names point to it, the file system frees the inode and blocks. But freeing isn't erasing: the data typically stays on the drive, just no longer listed, and its space is treated as free for the operating system to overwrite whenever it likes. Until that happens, recovery tools can often bring it back.

cards.headline: SSDs, and deleting for real
cards.body: Solid-state drives change the odds. With a command called TRIM, the operating system tells the drive which areas are no longer needed, and the drive's own background clean-up can then clear them, destroying deleted data. To truly clear a device, the UK's National Cyber Security Centre says hitting Delete isn't enough: overwrite all its memory, or use a factory reset that deletes the encryption keys.

title: Bugs
objective: After this level you can explain how a bug creeps into a program, from the 1947 moth to the 1996 Ariane 5 rocket failure.
summary: The 1947 moth was a literal bug, but the word was older. Ariane 5 was lost in 1996 when reused Ariane 4 software tried to fit a too-large number into 16 bits.

cards.headline: On 9 September 1947, a team found a moth inside a computer.
cards.body: They taped it into the logbook as the "First actual case of bug being found." The joke only works because engineers already called faults bugs. This level follows a far costlier bug, one with no wings at all.

mascot.line: People often say this moth gave us the word bug. It didn't: the joke in the logbook only works because the word already existed.

cards.headline: A real bug, but not the first "bug"
cards.body: The moth was caught between the relay contacts of the Harvard Mark II in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Grace Hopper was there, and she later made the story famous in her many talks. But the word was older: calling a technical fault a bug goes back to Thomas Edison in the 1800s. The moth didn't coin the term. It was just a very literal example of it.

cards.headline: Ariane 5: lost in under a minute
cards.body: On 4 June 1996, the first Ariane 5 rocket veered off its flight path, broke up and exploded about 40 seconds after its flight sequence began. The inquiry board found it had lost its guidance and attitude information 37 seconds after the main engine ignition sequence started. The cause was errors in the software of its inertial reference system, the unit that measures which way the rocket points and moves.

cards.headline: A number too big for its box
cards.body: That software was practically the same as Ariane 4's. It converted a 64-bit floating-point number into a 16-bit signed integer, and on Ariane 5's faster early trajectory, with much higher horizontal velocity, the value was too large to fit. The backup unit, identical in hardware and software, had already failed the same way. Code that was right for one rocket was wrong for the next.
cards.callout: 16 bits give 65,536 combinations. A number that runs out of bits overflows: there's nowhere left to carry.

title: Checkpoint: How Software Works
objective: After this level you can explain how a program is written, translated, run and shared out by the operating system, and how it goes wrong.
summary: Testing every multiplication on one machine would take about 30,000 years, so testing shows bugs but never their absence. Recap of code, translation, algorithms, the OS, files and bugs.

cards.headline: Can you test a program until you know it has no bugs?
cards.body: Chapter 3 finale. You've followed a program from exact steps to machine code, through the operating system to the drive, and watched bugs slip in. One question ties it all together: how would you ever know a program is right?

cards.headline: 30,000 years to test one multiplier
cards.body: The computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra once did the sums for his university's computer. Its words were 27 bits long, so it had 2 to the power 54 possible multiplications. At 2 to the power 14 a second, trying each one once would take about 30,000 years. It's Level 26's runaway growth again. His moral: "program testing can be used very effectively to show the presence of bugs but never to show their absence."

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one breath
cards.body: A program spells out every step, because a computer never guesses. People write it in a language suited to the job, and a compiler, interpreter or just-in-time compiler turns it into the processor's machine code. Inside, variables remember, ifs choose and loops repeat, and a good algorithm, like binary search, keeps the steps from exploding as data grows. The operating system shares out the processor and tracks files on the drive. And bugs creep in when an assumption, like a number's size, stops being true.

title: What a Network Is
objective: After this level you can explain how a home or office network links devices through a switch or router so they can share data.
summary: A local network links nearby devices. Each has a 48-bit MAC address; a switch learns which port each one is on, and a router joins networks together.

cards.headline: You press Print on your phone. How does the page find the right printer?
cards.body: It doesn't come out of the wrong device. Your home network has to deliver the job to one device out of many. This level opens up the small network in your home or office and shows how it knows which device is which.

cards.headline: A network is devices that can reach each other
cards.body: A local area network, or LAN, connects computers within a building or a small group of buildings: the laptop, phone, printer and TV in your home, or every desk in an office. Since the mid-1970s the most common LAN design has been Ethernet, first developed at Xerox PARC.

cards.headline: Every device wears a name tag
cards.body: Each network card carries a MAC address: 48 bits, or 6 bytes, written into its read-only memory at the factory. On the local network, that address identifies which device sent a message and which one should get it. Think of it as a name tag sewn in at the factory, though software can swap the tag a device shows.

cards.headline: The switch learns who sits where
cards.body: A switch is a box with a row of ports. Each time a frame (a chunk of data on the local network) comes in, the switch notes the sender's MAC address and the port it arrived on. Later frames for that address go out of that one port only. If the switch hasn't met the destination yet, it sends the frame out of every port except the one it came in on. It's a new mail clerk learning the office from the return addresses.

mascot.line: People mix these two up all the time. Switch: devices inside one network. Router: one network to the next.

cards.headline: Switches link devices; routers link networks
cards.body: A switch connects the devices inside one network. A router connects networks to each other, and your network to the internet, directing packets toward where they're going. Remember Level 1's network of networks? Routers are the joints between them.

title: IP Addresses
objective: After this level you can explain how every device online gets an IP address, and why IPv4's 4.3 billion addresses ran out.
summary: Every device directly online has an IP address; IPv4 writes its 32 bits as four numbers from 0 to 255, allowing about 4.3 billion, and the free pool ran dry in 2011.

cards.headline: IPv4 had room for about 4.3 billion addresses. The central pool ran out in 2011.
cards.body: Every device directly connected to the internet needs its own address, the way every house needs one for mail to arrive. So how is an internet address built, and how did the world run short of numbers?

cards.headline: An address for the whole internet
cards.body: Level 31's MAC address only works on your local network. To cross the internet, a packet uses an IP address, from the Internet Protocol, first set out in 1981. Every device directly connected to the internet has one, and every packet's header carries two of them: where it came from and where it's going. It's the internet's postal address, written on every envelope.

cards.headline: Four bytes, written as four numbers
cards.body: An IPv4 address is 32 bits long. People write it as four 8-bit parts, each a decimal number, separated by dots: 128.9.0.32, for example. Each part is one byte, and Level 2's byte has 256 patterns, so each number runs from 0 to 255. All 32 bits together allow 4,294,967,296 addresses, about 4.3 billion.

cards.fact: On February 3, 2011, IANA handed out the last free blocks in its central pool of IPv4 addresses.
cards.context: IANA, which manages the world's pool of addresses, gave its final blocks to the five regional internet registries, which kept handing out their remaining stock within their regions for years. The long-term fix is IPv6, whose addresses are 128 bits: 96 bits more than IPv4. Since each extra bit doubles the count, IPv6 allows a number of addresses 39 digits long.

title: DNS: The Internet's Phone Book
objective: After this level you can explain how DNS turns a name like example.com into the number address a computer can reach.
summary: DNS turns names into IP addresses: a resolver checks its cache, then asks a root server, the .com servers and the domain's own name servers in turn.

cards.headline: Once, one file listed every computer on the internet.
cards.body: It was called HOSTS.TXT. One office kept it, and every computer on the network copied it. As the network grew, that plan fell apart. Its replacement is the system you use every time you type a web address.

cards.headline: Names for people, numbers for machines
cards.body: Computers reach each other by IP address, but people remember names. The Domain Name System, DNS, turns a name like example.com into the IP address a computer can use. (That name is real, reserved just for examples like this one.) Your browser hands the question to a program called a resolver, which does the looking up.

cards.headline: Ask the root, then .com, then the owner
cards.body: A resolver with no saved answer starts at the top. A root server doesn't know example.com's address, but it knows who runs .com, so it replies with a referral to those servers. A .com server, in turn, refers the resolver to example.com's own name servers, which hold the actual address. Three questions, each narrowing it down, like asking the library desk, then the right floor, then the shelf.

cards.fact: 13 named root servers, run by 12 organizations, answer from more than 2,000 machines worldwide.
cards.context: Each name, a to m, is really many copies spread around the globe. Resolvers also keep a cache of answers they've looked up recently and check it before asking anyone, so most lookups never reach the root. That caching is what lets DNS keep up with the whole internet.

title: Routers Pass It On
objective: After this level you can explain how routers forward each packet one hop at a time, with no single machine knowing the whole route.
summary: Each router forwards a packet one hop by looking up its destination in a routing table; networks share routes over BGP, and a Time to Live countdown stops endless loops.

cards.headline: No router on the internet plans your packet's whole trip.
cards.body: Your packet passes through router after router on its way to a website, yet none of them works out the full route. Each one makes a single decision: where to send it next. So how does anything arrive?

cards.headline: One hop at a time
cards.body: When a packet arrives, a router reads its destination IP address and looks it up in its routing table, a list of which neighbor to use for which addresses. It sends the packet to that next hop and moves on. The next router does the same. It's a letter passed from post office to post office, each one only knowing which way to send it.

cards.headline: Networks tell each other where they reach
cards.body: Routing tables don't fill themselves. Between the separate networks that make up the internet, routers use BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, to tell each other which addresses each network can reach. Those announcements are what the tables are built from.

mascot.line: This is Level 2's byte again: 8 bits, so the countdown can never start higher than 255.

cards.headline: A countdown on every packet

When it hits zero, the router throws the packet away and sends a note back to the sender. That keeps a packet caught in a routing loop from circling forever.

title: Lost Packets and Second Tries
objective: After this level you can explain how TCP numbers packets, checks that all of them arrived and asks again for missing ones.
summary: IP promises nothing, so TCP opens with a three-way handshake, numbers every byte, acknowledges what arrived and resends what did not; UDP skips all that.

cards.headline: The internet's delivery service makes no promises.
cards.body: IP, which carries every packet, guarantees nothing: packets can arrive damaged, duplicated, out of order or not at all. Yet your downloads arrive perfect. Something at each end is keeping score.

cards.headline: A three-way handshake
cards.body: Before any data flows, TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, opens a connection with three messages. Your device sends a SYN: "let's talk, and here's the number I'll start counting from." The server answers with a SYN-ACK: "got it, and here's my starting number." Your device replies ACK. Now both sides agree where the counting starts.

cards.headline: Every byte gets a number
cards.body: TCP numbers every byte it sends, not just every packet. The receiver answers with an acknowledgment naming the next byte it expects, which means "I have everything before this." Bytes that arrive out of order drop back into place by their numbers, and a copy that arrives twice gives itself away.

cards.headline: No reply? Send it again
cards.body: The sender keeps track of what hasn't been acknowledged yet. If no acknowledgment arrives before a timer runs out, it sends that data again. Each packet also carries a checksum, so a packet damaged on the way fails the check and gets treated as lost. Perfect delivery, built on top of an imperfect network.

cards.fact: UDP, the other main transport protocol, skips the handshake and never resends lost data.
cards.context: It sends messages with a bare minimum of rules, and delivery isn't guaranteed. Its own specification tells programs that need reliable, in-order delivery to use TCP instead.

title: Layers: Envelopes in Envelopes
objective: After this level you can explain how internet protocols wrap data in layers, each layer doing one job for the one above.
summary: Internet protocols stack four layers (application, transport, internet, link); sending wraps data in each layer's header, and the receiver unwraps them in reverse.

cards.headline: Your message leaves your phone inside envelopes inside envelopes.
cards.body: By the time a chat message goes out, several pieces of software have each wrapped it in a label of their own. Each does one job and passes it on. Unwrapping them tells you how the whole internet is organized.

cards.headline: Four layers, four jobs
cards.body: The internet's rulebook, from 1989, stacks four layers. Application: the program's own message, such as an email. Transport: TCP or UDP, carrying it end to end between programs. Internet: IP, moving it from the source computer to the destination computer across networks. Link: the rules of whatever local network it's crossing right now.

cards.headline: Wrap on the way down, unwrap on the way up
cards.body: Each layer wraps what it gets from above with its own header. TCP adds port numbers, ordering information and a checksum, making a segment. IP adds the sending and receiving IP addresses. The link layer adds a header and an error-checking footer, making a frame. On arrival, each layer strips off the header its twin added at the sender and passes the rest up.

mascot.line: People mix these two up all the time. OSI is a seven-layer model; the internet itself was built on four. Same idea, different slicing.

title: Light in Glass: Fiber Optics
objective: After this level you can explain how fiber optic cables carry data as pulses of light kept inside thin strands of glass.
summary: Fiber traps light in a glass core by reflection off lower-index cladding. Kao's 1966 insight that pure glass was the key took signals from 20 meters to over 100 km.

cards.headline: In the 1960s, light in a glass fiber faded out after about 20 meters.
cards.body: Today it carries the internet across oceans. The breakthrough wasn't a cleverer cable design. It was cleaner glass, and one scientist's calculation of how clean it needed to be.

cards.headline: Light that can't get out
cards.body: Light passing from water into air can bounce back into the water instead of escaping, because water has a higher refractive index (a measure of how much a material bends light). A fiber uses the same trick: a glass core is wrapped in cladding glass with a lower refractive index, so light hitting the edge reflects back in and zigzags along. A long-distance core is about 10 micrometers across, thinner than a hair.

cards.headline: Kao's bet on pure glass
cards.body: In 1966, Charles Kao, working with George Hockham, showed that the real problem was impurities in the glass soaking up the light, not flaws in the fiber. With the purest glass, he calculated, signals could travel over 100 kilometers instead of 20 meters. Kao hoped 1 percent of the light would survive a kilometer. Today about 95 percent does. He shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work.

cards.context: Electrical signals are turned into light at one end and back at the other. Even pure glass dims the light a little, so long links use optical amplifiers that boost the light directly, without turning it back into electricity along the way.

title: One Address, Many Devices
objective: After this level you can explain how your home router shares one public address among all your devices.
summary: Homes use reusable private addresses; the router swaps them for its one public address and a port, keeps a table to route replies back, and conserves IPv4.

cards.headline: Your laptop, phone and TV share one internet address.
cards.body: To the rest of the internet, every device in your home looks like the same single address. That trick has helped stretch IPv4's limited supply of addresses. Here's how your router pulls it off.

cards.headline: Private addresses, reused everywhere
cards.body: IANA set aside three blocks of addresses for private networks, including every address that starts with 192.168. Anyone may use them without asking a registry, so many networks reuse the very same numbers. The catch: a private address is only unique inside its own network, so the internet can't reach it directly.

mascot.line: Keep this: private addresses inside, one public address outside, and a table in the router remembering who asked for what.

cards.headline: The router rewrites the envelope
cards.body: When your laptop sends a packet out, the router swaps its private address for the router's own public one, and swaps the laptop's port (a 16-bit number labeling that conversation) for one the router picks. It writes the swap in a table. When a reply comes back to that port, the router looks it up, swaps the originals back in and passes it inside. This is network address translation, or NAT.

cards.headline: A door that opens outward
cards.body: Because the table fills only when a device inside starts a conversation, NAT sessions normally begin from inside. A packet arriving from outside, unasked, finds no entry, unless the router was set up in advance with a fixed rule for it. Meanwhile, every home sharing one public address leaves others free: using private addresses conserves the public ones and stretches IPv4's life.

title: The Last Mile
objective: After this level you can compare how homes connect to the internet by cable, fiber, cell networks and low-orbit satellites.
summary: The last mile reaches homes by DSL over phone lines, cable over TV coax, fiber, or radio; geostationary satellites hover far away while low-orbit ones need big constellations.

cards.headline: Every home needs its own last mile.
cards.body: Your data's trip starts with one short link: the last mile, from your home or business to the local network provider. It can be built from very different stuff: old phone wire, TV cable, glass or radio.

cards.headline: Wires that were already there
cards.body: DSL, the digital subscriber line, sends data over the copper telephone line, and the line still works for calls at the same time. Cable internet uses the same coaxial cable that brings TV pictures and sound. Fiber to the home runs Level 37's glass right to the building, and fiber carries data much faster than DSL or cable.

cards.headline: Radio instead of wire
cards.body: Wireless links skip the cable altogether. Fixed wireless sends data from a local antenna to one on your home or business, much like DSL or cable but through the air. Mobile broadband reaches phones wherever they go. Satellites serve remote and thinly populated places.

cards.fact: A geostationary satellite orbits 35,786 km up, where one lap takes as long as one turn of the Earth.
cards.context: So it seems to hover over one spot, and three can cover the whole Earth. The catch is distance: data has to travel all the way up and back down, so users can notice more lag than with other kinds of internet link.

cards.headline: Closer, faster, and many more of them
cards.body: Low Earth orbit satellites fly below 2,000 km, so data's trip up and back is far shorter and the lag smaller. The trade-off: each one races across the sky and stays in view of a home only for a while. Keeping everyone covered takes a constellation of hundreds to thousands of satellites.

title: Asking for a Page
objective: After this level you can explain the request and response behind every web page, and why the web was built to forget you between requests.
summary: Every page starts with an HTTP request and a response with a status code. HTTP is stateless by design: servers forget each request so they can serve more people.

cards.headline: Every web page starts with a note: please send me this.
cards.body: Click a link and your browser sends a short message to a computer somewhere else. A moment later, a reply comes back. It happens for every page you open, and it has one strange feature: the server forgets you the instant it answers.

cards.headline: Request, response
cards.body: The web runs on HTTP, the rules for how browsers and servers talk. Your browser always starts: it sends a request, and the server answers with a response. To fetch a page, the request usually uses the method GET, which simply means "send me this". The response carries a status code: 200 means it worked; 404 means the server couldn't find what you asked for. So that's what the error page is quoting.

cards.headline: A server with no memory
cards.body: HTTP is stateless: there is no link between two requests, even two in a row on the same connection. So each request must carry everything the server needs to understand it. Ask for page one, then page two, and to the server you are a stranger both times. It sounds rude. It's actually the design.

cards.headline: Why build a web that forgets?
cards.body: Computer scientist Roy Fielding set out the reasoning in his 2000 description of the web's architecture. A server that keeps nothing between requests can free its resources the moment it answers, so it can serve far more people and recover more easily when something fails partway. The price is repetition: every request resends details the server could have remembered. Level 43 shows how sites win their memory back.

title: Cookies
objective: After this level you can explain why websites use cookies to remember you, and how third-party cookies follow you across sites.
summary: A cookie is data a server gives your browser to send back, letting a stateless web keep sessions. Third-party cookies from embedded content can follow you across sites.

cards.headline: The web forgets you after every click. So how does your cart remember?
cards.body: Level 41's servers keep no memory between requests. Yet you put shoes in a basket, open three more pages, and the shoes are still there. The trick is a small note that your own browser carries back and forth.

cards.headline: A note the browser hands back
cards.body: A cookie is a small piece of data a server sends to your browser. The browser stores it and sends it back to the same server with later requests. Since each request now carries the cookie, the server can link them into one session. Staying signed in, keeping a shopping cart, remembering your language or theme: all cookie jobs. The web still forgets; you just keep reminding it.

cards.headline: Cookies from someone else
cards.body: A cookie from the site in your address bar is first-party. One from any other domain is third-party, usually set by something embedded in the page, such as an ad. Now picture the same ad company embedded on a news site, a shoe shop and a recipe blog. Your browser hands it its cookie on all three, so it can build a profile of your browsing history and habits.

cards.fact: Safari and Firefox limit third-party cookies by default.
cards.context: Browser makers know people dislike being followed from site to site. Firefox goes a step further and gives each site its own separate cookie jar, so a cookie picked up on one site isn't handed over on another.

title: Why the Cloud Won
objective: After this level you can explain why companies rent computing from cloud providers instead of running their own servers, and what they give up.
summary: Cloud computing swaps buying servers for elastic, metered capacity that follows demand, cheaper through economies of scale; the price is control, while responsibility stays with you.

cards.headline: Own the computers, or rent them?
cards.body: Owning means buying machines up front, before you know exactly how busy you'll be. Renting from a cloud provider turns that big purchase into running costs that follow what you actually use. So why did renting win so many companies over, and what do they trade away?

cards.headline: Pay for what you use
cards.body: NIST, the US standards agency, lists what makes a service a cloud. Two features matter most for the bill. Rapid elasticity: capacity can be added and released quickly, sometimes automatically, as demand rises and falls, so to the customer it can seem unlimited. Measured service: storage, processing and bandwidth are metered, like electricity. Busy week? Rent more. Quiet night? Hand it back.

cards.headline: Why sharing is cheaper
cards.body: A cloud provider pools its machines to serve many customers, gaining economies of scale that a single company can't reach alone. For the customer, the cloud swaps a large capital investment in computers for operating costs that track real use, and it can lower the up-front cost of launching something new. No room full of idle servers required.

cards.headline: What you give up
cards.body: Control. Moving to a public cloud hands control of data and systems to the provider, and NIST warns that the customer then depends on the provider's cooperation for jobs like monitoring and responding to incidents. Yet the customer stays accountable for the security and privacy of what it moved. You can rent the computers. You can't rent out the responsibility.

title: Inside a Data Center
objective: After this level you can explain why data centers need so much electricity and cooling, and why that shapes where they are built.
summary: Most of a data center's electricity ends up as heat. PUE scores the overhead of removing it, and cool air and water for cooling help decide where data centers are built.

cards.headline: A data center is a giant computer that's also a giant heater.
cards.body: Most of the electricity a data center draws ends up as heat. So running one is really two jobs: powering the computers, and getting rid of what they give off. That second job shapes a surprising amount, right down to where on the map it's built.

cards.fact: US data centers used about 4.4% of the country's electricity in 2023.
cards.context: That's about 176 terawatt-hours, according to a 2024 report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The servers do the computing, and most of that energy then has to leave the building as heat.

cards.headline: A score for overhead: PUE
cards.body: Engineers rate a data center with PUE, power usage effectiveness: the energy the whole facility uses divided by the energy that reaches the computing equipment. A perfect 1.0 would mean every watt goes to computing and none to fans, chillers or lights. The US Department of Energy's 2024 guide puts an average data center at about 1.6, with some very efficient ones below 1.1. At 1.6, each watt of computing drags about 0.6 watts of overhead along.

cards.headline: Why cool places win
cards.body: When the outside air is cooler than the air leaving the servers, a data center can use it instead of running chillers, a trick called free cooling. Many data centers in cool climates use only that. Where cooling towers are used instead, they shed heat by evaporating water, so water use climbs with the heat the computers make. Cold air and enough water are questions of location.

title: Why Fast Internet Still Lags

summary: Bandwidth is how much data per second; latency is how long it takes to arrive. Light in fiber needs about 28 ms from New York to London, and no faster plan removes that.

cards.headline: You upgraded to a faster plan. Pages still pause before they load.

cards.headline: Distance you can't buy off
cards.body: Data in fiber travels as light, and glass slows light down: about 4.9 microseconds per kilometer instead of 3.34 in a vacuum. New York to London is about 5,585 km, so light in fiber needs about 28 milliseconds one way and 56 for a round trip. More bandwidth widens the hose. It can't shorten the ocean.

That's why engineers say latency, not bandwidth, is the bottleneck for most websites. Their fixes: make fewer round trips, and move the data closer to you.

title: Copies Near You
objective: After this level you can explain why popular videos and pages are copied to servers close to viewers, and what that saves.
summary: Content delivery networks keep copies of popular files on servers near viewers. Netflix's Open Connect puts servers inside internet providers and fills them off-peak.

cards.headline: Why send the same video across an ocean a million times?
cards.body: Level 46 showed that distance costs time, however fast your plan. So the busiest services beat distance the obvious way: they keep copies of popular files close to the people who want them.

cards.headline: A network of copies
cards.body: A content delivery network, or CDN, is a group of servers spread across many locations. They store duplicate copies of data, and each request is answered by a server close to the person asking. The trips are shorter, so pages and videos arrive sooner, and because the work is spread out, a sudden crowd of visitors hurts less.

cards.headline: Netflix's version: servers inside your provider
cards.body: Netflix runs its own CDN, called Open Connect. It offers internet providers its own servers to install inside their networks, free to qualifying providers, keeping video close to viewers. Because Netflix can predict what people will watch and when, it copies most new content onto those servers during off-peak hours. By the time you press play, the show has usually made the long trip already.

cards.headline: Level 9's trick, city-sized
cards.body: This is the cache idea from Level 9 again. A processor keeps copies of data in a small, fast cache because programs ask for the same things over and over. A CDN keeps copies near viewers for the same reason: many people ask for the same page or video. Each Netflix server inside a provider also takes a large amount of traffic off the links between that provider and other networks.

title: Squeezing Data: Compression
objective: After this level you can explain why photos and video can shrink to a fraction of their size, and what lossy compression throws away.
summary: Lossless compression removes repetition and restores data exactly; lossy compression like JPEG discards detail the eye misses; video stores only what changes between frames.

cards.headline: Level 3's photo: about 73 MB of pixels, about 3.6 MB as a JPEG.
cards.body: The saved file is about a twentieth of the raw pixels, and it still looks sharp. Where did the rest go? Some of it was repetition, and some of it was detail your eyes were never going to miss.

cards.headline: Lossless: say it shorter
cards.body: Lossless compression can be reversed to give back the original data exactly. It works by cutting repetition. The simplest trick, run-length encoding, replaces a run of repeated items with a count and one copy: instead of the same white pixel over and over, store how many, then one white pixel. Zip files are lossless, which matters for text, where every character has to come back exactly.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: lossless gives back every bit exactly. Lossy gives back something that only looks or sounds the same.

cards.headline: Lossy: drop what you won't see
cards.body: Lossy compression goes further and loses some detail for good. JPEG averages out small variations in color and throws away what the human eye cannot see, which is how Level 3's photo shrank about 20 to 1 with practically invisible loss. That works for pictures and voices, where small errors spread over scattered spots are hard to notice. On your bank statement, it would be a disaster.

title: Why Websites Go Down
objective: After this level you can explain why outages happen and how one small change can spread, using the 2021 Facebook outage.
summary: On October 4, 2021, a maintenance command cut Facebook's backbone, its DNS servers withdrew their routes, and Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp vanished for about six hours.

cards.headline: October 4, 2021: Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp vanished for about six hours.
cards.body: Not an attack. Meta called it an error of its own making, and it began with a single command during routine maintenance. Following how one mistake spread is the clearest lesson in why big websites go down.

cards.headline: Step 1: the backbone goes dark
cards.body: Facebook's data centers are linked by its own backbone network. During maintenance, a command meant to check how much backbone capacity was available accidentally took down every connection in it. An audit tool was supposed to stop commands like that, but a bug in the tool let it through. The data centers were cut off from each other and from the internet.

cards.headline: Step 2: the address book disappears
cards.body: DNS is the internet's address book: it turns a name like facebook.com into a server's IP address. Networks announce which addresses they can reach using BGP. Facebook's DNS servers were built to withdraw their BGP announcements if they lost touch with the data centers, and they did. So they became unreachable, though still running. To the rest of the world, Facebook was simply gone.

cards.headline: Step 3: locked out of the fix
cards.body: The outage also knocked out many of the internal tools Meta's engineers used every day, which made it harder to diagnose. Engineers had to go to the data centers in person, where buildings designed to be hard to get into, and hardware designed to be hard to change, slowed the repair. Meta said practice drills helped it bring things back carefully. One small change, then a cascade: every system leaned on the one before.
