title: Milestone: One Web Page, Start to Finish
objective: After this level you can explain every step from typing a web address to seeing the page: bits, software, DNS, packets, servers and your browser.
summary: From Enter to pixels: DNS finds the server, a handshake connects, GET fetches the HTML, more requests fetch its files, and the browser lays out and paints the page.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Follow one web page from Enter to screen.
cards.body: Your browser finds a server, asks for a page, collects the pieces and paints them onto your screen. You've now met almost every part of that trip. Here it is in order, from the key you press to the pixels you see.

events.label: DNS lookup: the site's name becomes the server's IP address
A TCP handshake opens a connection; HTTPS adds a TLS handshake
The browser sends a GET request, usually for the HTML
The HTML names style sheets, scripts and images: more requests
The browser builds the page's structure, styles and layout
Paint: every laid-out box becomes pixels on your screen

cards.headline: Every step leans on something you know
cards.body: The request and response are Level 41's, and a cookie reminds the forgetful server who you are. A nearby CDN copy trims the latency of each round trip, and JPEG compression keeps the photos small by dropping detail your eyes won't miss. At the very end, the browser converts each box into actual pixels: red, green and blue numbers from 0 to 255, straight out of Chapter 1.

cards.headline: Milestone: one page, end to end
learned: How bits, gates and a processor's endless loop turn stored numbers into text, pictures and sums.
How computing moved from punched cards and rewired cables to stored programs on transistor chips.
How code people write is translated into machine code and shared out by the operating system.
How DNS, routers and TCP carry every piece of a web page to you, complete and in order.
Why a page arrives as many requests, and why distance, cookies and nearby copies shape how it loads.

options.label: It copies the address from one master file listing every computer
options.rationale: That single file was dropped as the network grew; DNS replaced it.

options.label: It sends the name to every router until one of them recognizes it
options.rationale: Routers forward packets by address; they don't look up names.

options.label: It asks a root server, then the .com servers, then the site's own servers
It works the address out from the letters of the name itself
options.rationale: Names and addresses are unrelated; the mapping has to be looked up.

questions.explanation: Each server refers the resolver one step closer: the root knows who runs .com, and .com knows the site's own name servers.

options.label: The first request always fails and has to be repeated
options.rationale: The first request usually succeeds; more files are needed.

options.label: The HTML names style sheets, scripts and images it still needs
Each request can only carry one word of the page at a time
options.rationale: A response can carry a whole file.

options.label: The server asks the browser to send its cookies separately
options.rationale: Cookies ride along with each request.

questions.explanation: The HTML refers to other files (CSS, scripts, images), and the browser requests each one.

options.label: It sends every packet twice, in case one copy goes missing
options.rationale: TCP resends only what isn't acknowledged, not everything.

options.label: Each router keeps a copy until the next router confirms it
options.rationale: Routers forward and move on; the two ends keep score.

options.label: It hands the data to UDP, which guarantees it will arrive
options.rationale: UDP never resends lost data.

options.label: It numbers the bytes and resends any that aren't acknowledged

questions.explanation: The receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects; anything unacknowledged when the timer runs out is sent again.

options.label: How many bits the line can move each second
options.rationale: That's bandwidth, which the plan increases.

options.label: The delay set by the distance to the server
How much data it can download in an hour
options.rationale: That grows with bandwidth.

options.label: The width of the pipe the data flows through
options.rationale: The pipe's width is what bandwidth measures.

questions.explanation: Light in fiber needs time to cover the distance, about 28 ms from New York to London, whatever the bandwidth.

options.label: The processor reads the JavaScript itself, line by line
options.rationale: Only machine code runs on a processor.

options.label: The server sends a finished machine code file instead
options.rationale: Scripts arrive as source code; the browser translates them.

options.label: Its engine compiles them into machine code as the page runs
It skips them, since a browser can only show HTML
options.rationale: Browsers run scripts; that's what makes pages interactive.

questions.explanation: Every major browser engine has a just-in-time compiler that turns JavaScript into machine code while the page runs.

options.label: Keeping the program in memory, right beside its data
Resetting cables and switches for each new problem
options.rationale: That was ENIAC's way, and it took days per job.

options.label: Replacing hot vacuum tubes with small transistors
options.rationale: A better switch, not a way to change programs.

options.label: Feeding each new job in on a stack of punched cards
options.rationale: Cards fed data in from outside; the idea here is memory.

questions.explanation: In a stored-program computer, instructions are just more data in memory, so a new job means loading new instructions.

options.label: One letter code, such as ASCII 72
options.rationale: That's how text is stored, not a pixel's color.

options.label: A single bit that is either on or off
options.rationale: One bit gives only two options.

options.label: Red, green and blue values, each from 0 to 255
A tiny compressed JPEG file of its own

title: Why Updates Matter
objective: After this level you can explain why all complex software has security holes, what a zero-day is, and why installing updates quickly matters.
summary: All software has holes, some unknown even to its maker (zero-days). Patches close them, but attackers target unpatched machines for years, as WannaCry showed in 2017.

cards.headline: The fix was out two months before the attack.
cards.body: On May 12, 2017, the WannaCry ransomware began hitting computers, including machines at dozens of NHS trusts in England. The strange part: Microsoft had released a fix for the flaw it used back in March. Why do fixes come before attacks, and why doesn't everyone install them?

cards.headline: Every big program has holes
cards.body: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre puts it bluntly: all systems contain vulnerabilities, flaws an attacker could use. Some are known to the maker. Others nobody has found yet, or only an attacker has. An attack on one of those is called a zero-day, and the name tells the story: the maker has had zero days to fix it.

cards.headline: The race after a patch
cards.body: Once a maker learns of a flaw, it ships a patch: an update that fixes it. Your machine is safe from that flaw only after the patch is installed, and not everyone installs it. CISA, the US cyber defense agency, warns that attackers go after known holes for months or even years after the fix is out.

cards.headline: WannaCry: the gap in action
cards.body: Microsoft fixed the flaw WannaCry used on March 14, 2017. WannaCry arrived on May 12 and hit computers that had not applied the fix. In England, at least 81 of 236 NHS trusts were affected, and the infected organisations were running unpatched or unsupported Windows. So CISA's advice is simple: install updates as soon as possible, and turn on automatic updates so you don't have to remember.

cards.headline: Holes: patched
learned: All systems contain vulnerabilities, some unknown to their makers
A zero-day is a flaw the maker has had zero days to fix
Attackers target known holes for months or years after a patch
WannaCry (2017) hit machines that skipped a two-month-old fix

questions.prompt: What makes a software attack a "zero-day" attack?

options.label: It is launched on the first day a program goes on sale
options.rationale: The name is about the fix, not the sales date.

options.label: It does no damage until a day has passed
options.rationale: Zero-day is about how long the maker has had to fix the flaw.

options.label: It uses a flaw the maker did not yet know about
It only works on computers set to the wrong date
options.rationale: It has nothing to do with the clock.

questions.explanation: A zero-day attack exploits a previously unknown flaw, so the maker has had zero days to fix it.

questions.prompt: Why could WannaCry spread in May 2017 when a fix had existed since March?

options.label: Many computers had not installed the March update
The March fix only worked on phones
options.rationale: The fix was a Windows update; unpatched Windows machines were hit.

options.label: WannaCry used a brand-new zero-day flaw
options.rationale: The flaw was already known and fixed in March.

options.label: Updates cannot fix security flaws
options.rationale: A patch is exactly an update that fixes security flaws.

questions.explanation: WannaCry hit computers that had not applied Microsoft's March 14 fix; infected NHS organisations ran unpatched or unsupported Windows.

questions.prompt: Level 1 said a processor's switches have no idea what they are doing and simply follow software. Why does that make a flaw in the software matter?

options.label: The switches spot bad instructions and refuse them
options.rationale: The switches have no idea what the data means; software does the telling.

options.label: Flaws only matter in hardware, never in software
options.rationale: All systems, software included, contain vulnerabilities.

options.label: A software flaw fixes itself when the switches restart
options.rationale: Flaws stay until a patch fixes them.

options.label: The hardware carries out the software, flaws and all

questions.explanation: Hardware does the work and software gives the orders, so a flaw in the orders is a flaw an attacker can use.

title: How Sites Store Passwords
objective: After this level you can explain why a well-run site keeps only a scrambled hash of your password, never the password itself.
summary: A good site stores a salted, deliberately slow hash of your password: a one-way jumble it can check at login but cannot turn back into the password.

cards.headline: A good website doesn't know your password.
cards.body: Yet it can tell, every time, whether you typed the right one. It sounds like a magic trick. It's really a smart way of checking a secret without keeping it, and it matters most on the day a site gets robbed.

cards.headline: The blender
cards.body: A hash function takes input of any length, a word or a whole book, and turns out a jumble of fixed length. It works one way only: working back from the jumble to the input is computationally infeasible. Think of a blender. Strawberries go in, a smoothie comes out, and nobody is getting the strawberries back.

cards.headline: Checking without knowing
cards.body: So a well-run site stores only the hash of your password. When you log in, it hashes whatever you just typed and compares the two jumbles. Match, and the door opens. A thief who copies the site's password list gets smoothies, not passwords.

mascot.line: People mix these two up all the time. Encryption locks and unlocks with a key. A hash never unlocks at all.

cards.headline: Hashing is not encryption
cards.body: Encryption is two-way: with the key, scrambled text turns back into the original. Hashing is one-way: there's no key and nothing to decrypt. For passwords, that's the whole point. If a site encrypted your password instead, anyone who got hold of the key could read it.

cards.headline: A pinch of salt, and a slow blender
cards.body: Identical passwords would give identical hashes, and attackers keep ready-made tables of hashes for common passwords. So sites add a salt: a unique random value mixed into each password before hashing. Now identical passwords get different hashes and the tables are useless. Good sites also choose a deliberately slow hash, because a fast one lets a thief test guesses at great speed. NIST, the US standards agency, requires passwords to be stored salted and hashed.

cards.headline: Passwords: blended
learned: A hash turns any input into a fixed-length, one-way jumble
Sites hash what you type and compare it with the stored hash
Hashing is one-way; encryption can be undone with a key
Salts and slow hashes make stolen hashes hard to crack

questions.prompt: What does a well-run website keep so it can check your password at login?

options.label: Your password, written in a locked file
options.rationale: Keeping the password itself is exactly what good sites avoid.

options.label: Only a hash of your password
The first three letters of your password
options.rationale: It stores a hash of the whole password.

options.label: Nothing; it asks your email provider each time
options.rationale: The site checks against the hash it stores.

questions.explanation: The site stores only the hash; at login it hashes what you type and compares the two.

questions.prompt: Why does a site add a unique random salt to each password before hashing it?

options.label: To make passwords easier for you to remember
options.rationale: You never see the salt; it works behind the scenes.

options.label: So the hash can be decrypted if you forget your password
options.rationale: Hashes are one-way; salt does not change that.

options.label: So identical passwords get different hashes and ready-made tables fail
To make the stored hash shorter
options.rationale: A hash has a fixed length anyway.

questions.explanation: With a unique salt, two people with the same password get different hashes, and precomputed tables of hashes stop working.

questions.prompt: Level 51 said all systems contain vulnerabilities. Why does a site storing only hashes still matter if it is well built?

options.label: Because hashes stop every attack on the site from ever happening
options.rationale: Hashing limits the damage; it does not prevent every break-in.

options.label: Because if a flaw lets a thief copy the list, they get hashes, not passwords
Because hashing patches the site's software flaws automatically
options.rationale: Patches fix flaws; hashing protects the stored passwords.

options.label: Because well-built sites never have flaws
options.rationale: All systems contain vulnerabilities, even good ones.

questions.explanation: Since every system can have holes, sites plan for a break-in: a stolen list of hashes does not reveal the passwords.

title: Why Long Passwords Win
objective: After this level you can explain why each extra character multiplies an attacker's guesses, and why one reused password unlocks many accounts.
summary: Every extra character multiplies an attacker's guesses, which matters when stolen hashes can be tested by the billion; but common passwords go first, and a reused one opens every account.

cards.headline: Add one character and the guessing job gets many times bigger.
cards.body: Password advice can sound like superstition: add a symbol, swap an e for a 3. The arithmetic tells a cleaner story, and it points to two habits that matter more than any clever swap.

cards.headline: Every character multiplies
cards.body: A 4-digit passcode has 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 = 10,000 possibilities. Add a fifth digit and there are 100,000. Use four letters, upper and lower case, and it's 52 x 52 x 52 x 52: over 7 million. Each extra character multiplies the possibilities instead of adding to them. It's Level 2's rule again, where each extra bit doubles the patterns, only with a bigger multiplier.

cards.headline: Why the math matters after a breach
cards.body: Remember Level 52's stolen hashes? Thieves who have them can guess offline, with no login page to slow them down, and NIST notes they can compute many billions of hashes per second. Against that speed a short password falls quickly, while every extra character multiplies the work. That's why NIST calls length a primary factor in password strength.

cards.headline: Guessers don't start at aaaa
cards.body: Attackers try the likely passwords first: dictionary words and passwords leaked in earlier breaches. NIST says sites should block those. So length only helps if the password isn't a common one. CISA suggests a passphrase of 4 to 7 unrelated words, a different one for every account, kept in a password manager.

cards.headline: One key, many doors
cards.body: Why a different password everywhere? Credential stuffing: attackers take username and password pairs leaked from one website and try them on other websites. Reuse one password, and a breach at a shop you forgot about could hand over your email account too.

cards.headline: Passwords: stretched
learned: Each extra character multiplies the possible passwords
Stolen hashes can be tested by the billion per second offline
Common and leaked passwords are tried first
Credential stuffing turns one reused password into many break-ins

questions.prompt: A 4-digit passcode has 10,000 possible codes. How many does a 5-digit passcode have?

options.rationale: An extra digit multiplies the count; it does not add one.
That would be doubling, but each digit has 10 choices.
Each extra digit multiplies by 10.

questions.explanation: Each extra digit multiplies the possibilities by 10: 10,000 x 10 = 100,000.

questions.prompt: Why does reusing one password across many sites put all of those accounts at risk?

options.label: Websites share their password lists with each other
options.rationale: Attackers carry leaked pairs from site to site, not the sites.

options.label: Reused passwords get shorter each time they are used
options.rationale: A password does not change by being reused.

options.label: Attackers try pairs leaked from one site on other sites
Hashing stops working when a password is reused
options.rationale: Hashing still works; the leaked pair is simply tried elsewhere.

questions.explanation: Credential stuffing tries username and password pairs leaked from one website on other websites.

questions.prompt: Each extra bit doubles the patterns. What does each extra character, chosen from 52 letters, do to the possible passwords?

options.label: Adds 52 more possibilities
options.rationale: Characters multiply the count, as bits do.

options.label: Doubles them, just like a bit
options.rationale: A bit has 2 choices; a letter here has 52.

options.label: Leaves them the same if it is a letter
options.rationale: Every extra character multiplies the count.

options.label: Multiplies them by 52

questions.explanation: A bit has 2 choices, so each bit doubles; a character from 52 letters has 52 choices, so each one multiplies by 52.

title: Two-Factor and Passkeys
objective: After this level you can explain why a second factor, or a passkey that never leaves your device, stops most stolen-password attacks.
summary: Multifactor authentication adds a second kind of proof, so a stolen password alone fails; codes can still be phished, but passkeys keep the private key on your device and work only on the real site.

cards.headline: Someone has your password. Now what?
cards.body: Maybe it leaked in a breach. Maybe you typed it into the wrong page. With a password alone, that's game over. Add one more lock, and the stolen password stops being enough.

cards.headline: Know, have, are
cards.body: Multifactor authentication, often called two-factor, asks for two or more kinds of proof: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone or a security key) or something you are (a fingerprint or face). With it switched on, a thief who stole only your password is stuck at the second door.

cards.headline: Not all second doors are equal
cards.body: A fake login page can ask for your password and the 6-digit code from your phone at the same moment, then pass both straight on to the real site. That's why CISA ranks text and email codes as the weakest second factor and physical security keys as the best defense against phishing. Still, any second factor beats none.

cards.headline: Passkeys: nothing to steal
cards.body: A passkey swaps the password for a pair of keys. The private key stays on your device, and you unlock it the way you unlock your phone. The website stores only the public key, so there's no password on its server to steal. And each passkey is bound to the real website, so a look-alike page gets nothing it can use.

cards.headline: Logins: doubled up
learned: MFA combines something you know, have and are
A stolen password alone can't open an MFA account
Phishing pages can relay codes; security keys resist that best
A passkey keeps its private key on your device and works only on the real site

options.label: Your name, your address and your birthday
options.rationale: Those are facts others can find; MFA uses know, have and are.

options.label: Three different passwords
options.rationale: Three passwords are all the same kind: something you know.

options.label: Something you know, have and are
A username, an email and a phone number
options.rationale: Those identify you; they do not prove it.

questions.explanation: MFA mixes kinds of proof: something you know, something you have and something you are.

options.label: Text codes never expire, so an old code still works later
options.rationale: The trick works in real time; expiry does not stop it.

options.label: It asks for your password and code together, then passes both on
Phones send the code to every website at once
options.rationale: The code goes only to you; the fake page asks you for it.

options.label: The code is the same for everyone
options.rationale: Each code is different, but you can be tricked into typing it.

questions.explanation: A fake page collects the password and the fresh code at the same moment and relays them to the real site.

options.label: The site stores only a public key, with no password at all
The site stores the private key in a stronger blender
options.rationale: The private key never goes to the site; it stays on your device.

options.label: Passkeys are hashed twice
options.rationale: A passkey replaces the password with a key pair.

options.label: The site deletes the passkey after each login
options.rationale: The site keeps the public key for next time.

questions.explanation: With a passkey the site holds just the public key, so a breach finds no password or hash to crack.

title: Public Keys: The Open Padlock
objective: After this level you can explain how public-key cryptography lets two strangers agree on a secret over a line anyone can hear.
summary: Public keys work like open padlocks: anyone can lock, only the private key opens. One-way math (RSA, 1977) keeps it safe, and it mainly sets up a faster session key.

cards.headline: How do you whisper a secret across a crowded room?
cards.body: To share a secret key privately, it seems you'd first need a private way to share the key. Public-key cryptography escapes that loop with one of the neatest tricks in computing. Picture an open padlock.

mascot.line: Keep this picture: the public key is an open padlock anyone can snap shut. The private key is the only one that opens it.

cards.headline: Hand out open padlocks
cards.body: Imagine giving open padlocks to anyone who asks. Anyone can put a note in a box and snap your padlock shut, but only you hold the key that opens it. That's the idea: a public key you publish, and a private key you keep. What the public key locks, only the private key unlocks. Diffie and Hellman's 1976 paper showed strangers could talk secretly this way over an open channel, with no secret arranged first.

cards.headline: Easy one way, brutal the other
cards.body: Why can't someone study the padlock and cut its key? RSA, introduced in 1977 by MIT's Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman, builds the keys from two huge prime numbers. Multiplying them is easy. Working back from the product to the two primes is far beyond what computers can do, and that's what keeps the private key private.

cards.headline: Padlock first, then a faster lock
cards.body: Public-key math is slow, so it mostly does one job: exchanging a session key. Your device can lock a fresh random key in the other side's padlock and send it across a line anyone can hear. From then on, both sides use that shared session key with faster encryption for the actual data.

cards.headline: Invented twice
cards.body: Diffie and Hellman went public in 1976, and RSA followed in 1977. But at Britain's code agency GCHQ, James Ellis, Clifford Cocks and Malcolm Williamson had worked out public-key methods earlier in the 1970s. Their work stayed classified until 1997.

cards.headline: Padlocks: handed out
learned: A public key locks; only the matching private key unlocks
Strangers can talk secretly with no secret arranged first
RSA rests on how hard it is to find two huge primes from their product
Public-key math mainly sets up a faster session key

options.label: The two keys are stored in different countries
options.rationale: Location is not what protects it; the math is.

options.label: Anyone who has the public key can unlock it
options.rationale: The public key only locks; it cannot open.

title: The Padlock in Your Browser
objective: After this level you can explain why HTTPS certificates prove you reached the real site, and what the browser padlock does not promise.
summary: HTTPS sets up a private, tamper-checked line; the certificate, signed by an authority that checked domain control, proves you reached the named site. It does not prove the site is honest.

cards.headline: The padlock by the web address says less than you might think.
cards.body: It's tempting to read that little icon as "this site is safe." It makes a narrower promise, and a very useful one. To see exactly what, follow what happens before it appears.

cards.headline: HTTPS: a private line
cards.body: HTTPS is ordinary web traffic secured by TLS. First comes a quick handshake in which your browser and the server agree on a secret session key, Level 55's trick at work. After that, every message is encrypted, headers included, and TLS detects any tampering on the way. It also lets the server prove who it is. That's the next card.

cards.headline: The certificate: a signed seal
cards.body: How do you know you reached the real bank.com and not an impostor? The site presents a certificate: a digitally signed copy of its public key, tied to its domain name. The signer is a certificate authority that browsers trust, and it signs only after the applicant proves it controls the domain, for example by posting a file or a DNS record the authority asks for.

cards.headline: What the padlock doesn't promise
cards.body: Notice what got checked: control of a name, not good character. Let's Encrypt, a widely used nonprofit certificate authority, issues certificates for free, and the FBI warns that phishing sites use HTTPS and the lock icon too. So the padlock means a private line to whoever controls that exact address. Whether that's who you think it is remains your call.

cards.headline: Padlock: read properly
learned: HTTPS is web traffic secured by TLS: encrypted and tamper-checked
A certificate ties a site's public key to its domain name
Authorities sign only after the site proves it controls the domain
The padlock proves the address, not the honesty of its owner

title: Viruses, Worms and Trojans
objective: After this level you can explain how viruses, worms and trojans differ in the way they get onto a computer and spread.
summary: Viruses ride inside other programs, worms spread themselves through security holes with no click, and trojans trick you into installing them; the 1988 Morris worm showed how fast worms move.

cards.headline: Three kinds of uninvited guest.
cards.body: Harmful software comes in families, named for how each one gets in. Know which is which, and you know which door to lock.

mascot.line: People call all of these viruses. The real difference is how they travel: riding along, crawling alone, or invited in.

cards.headline: Virus, worm, trojan: how each one gets in

items.label: Virus

items.label: Trojan

cards.headline: The trojan's trick
cards.body: The trojan is named for the Greek legend in which warriors hid inside a wooden horse to get into Troy, a story told in the Odyssey. The software works the same way. It looks like a useful program, so you install and launch it yourself, and its hidden harmful function runs along with it. No lock gets picked when you open the gate.

cards.headline: Why worms spread fastest
cards.body: A worm doesn't wait for anyone to click. It spreads itself, moving from computer to computer through holes in security, the kind that updates fix. In 1988 the Morris worm caused major problems for about 6,000 of the 60,000 computers then linked to the internet, roughly one in ten. That's Level 51's lesson at network speed: every unpatched hole is an open door.

title: Ransomware
objective: After this level you can explain why ransomware attacks hospitals, cities and companies, and why backups are the best defense.
summary: Ransomware encrypts a victim's files and sells back the key, squeezing organisations that cannot stop working; paying guarantees nothing, and offline backups make the key worthless.

cards.headline: Your files are still there. You just can't open them.
cards.body: That's the business model of ransomware: scramble a victim's data, then sell back the key. It hurts most where waiting is not an option.

cards.headline: Locked with a key you don't have
cards.body: Ransomware encrypts the files on a device, making them, and the systems that rely on them, unusable. Then the attackers demand payment to unlock them. Encryption is two-way, so the files can be unscrambled, but only by whoever holds the key. Here, that's the attacker.

cards.headline: Why hospitals and pipelines
cards.body: Ransomware can leave an organisation unable to reach the data it needs to operate and deliver critical services. When WannaCry struck in 2017, NHS England estimated over 19,000 appointments were cancelled. After an attack on May 7, 2021, Colonial Pipeline, which carries about 45% of the gasoline used on the US East Coast, halted fuel for nearly a week and paid a $4.4 million ransom.

cards.headline: Pay up?
cards.body: Paying is no sure thing. The FBI does not support paying a ransom: payment doesn't guarantee the data comes back, and it encourages more attacks. Many gangs also steal the data first and threaten to publish it unless the victim pays, so one attack becomes two threats.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level: a backup the ransomware can't reach turns the ransom note into scrap paper.

cards.headline: The best defense is a spare copy
cards.body: If you can restore your files yourself, the attacker's key is worthless. So CISA advises backups that are offline, encrypted and tested regularly. Offline matters: ransomware hunts for any backup it can reach and deletes or encrypts that too. A backup drive left plugged in can get locked along with everything else.

title: Phishing: Hacking the Human
objective: After this level you can explain why phishing works by rushing and tricking people rather than breaking code, and spot its signs.
summary: Phishing is social engineering: messages posing as someone you trust, pulling levers like urgency. Break the rush and verify another way; passkeys defeat even perfect fakes.

cards.headline: Why pick a lock when someone will hand you the key?
cards.body: Level 55's math is brutal to break. A person in a hurry is not. Phishing goes after the human, not the code.

cards.headline: Hacking the human
cards.body: Security people call it social engineering: tricking someone into revealing information, such as a password, that can be used to attack systems. Phishing is social engineering by message. An email, a text or a fake website poses as an organisation you trust, and fishes for your details.

cards.headline: Five levers
cards.body: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre lists the levers scammers pull: authority (a message that seems to come from your bank or the tax office), urgency (pay now or face a fine), emotion (fear or curiosity), scarcity (a deal about to vanish) and current events (whatever is in the news). Every lever does the same job: it pushes you to act before you think.

cards.headline: Slow down and go around
cards.body: So the defense is to break the rush. CISA's advice: if a request seems odd, contact the company directly, using contact details you already have, never the ones in the message. Technology helps too. Level 54's passkeys are bound to the real website, so even a flawless fake page gets nothing it can use.

title: Checkpoint: Security Online

cards.body: CISA, the US cyber defense agency, boils its everyday advice down to four steps in its Secure Our World campaign: recognize and report phishing, use strong passwords, turn on multifactor authentication and update software. Every one of them answers an attack from this chapter.

cards.headline: Why updates made the list
cards.body: CISA's reason for the fourth step is blunt: flaws in software can give criminals access to files or accounts, so don't delay updates. WannaCry is what losing that race looks like: it hit computers that had skipped a fix released two months earlier. Add Level 58's offline, tested backups, and even an attack that gets through can't hold your files hostage.

title: What a Database Is
objective: After this level you can explain how a database stores records in tables and uses an index to find one among billions.
summary: A database keeps records as rows in tables, with typed columns that give the data meaning, and an index that jumps straight to one row instead of scanning them all.

cards.headline: A computer just found your order in a blink. It didn't read every one.
cards.body: Shops, banks and apps keep their records in databases: collections of data organized so a computer can search them and pull out one entry fast. Chapter 7 is about your data, so start with where it lives. How do you find one row among a mountain of them?

cards.headline: Tables: rows and columns
cards.body: The most popular kind, the relational database, stores data in tables, much like a spreadsheet. Each row is one record, say one customer, and each column is one field of that record: name, address, date joined. The columns are fixed; the rows come and go. Sign up for a new app and, somewhere, a table grows by exactly one row. That row is you.

cards.headline: Every column has a type
cards.body: Each column also has a data type, such as whole numbers, text or dates. The type limits what can go in the column and gives the stored data its meaning, so the database knows a number column can be added up and a date column can be compared with other dates. The same bits in a text column would just be letters. The table's design tells the database how to read every cell.

cards.fact: Without an index, a database must check every row, one by one.
cards.context: An index works like the one at the back of a book: look up the term, flip straight to the page. A database index keeps one column's values in sorted order, each pointing to its row, so searching it is much faster than searching the table. The price is upkeep: every change to the table must update the index too, so indexes nobody uses get removed.

title: The Data Your Phone Gives Off
objective: After this level you can connect cookies, apps and location settings to the data trail your phone leaves in a normal day.
summary: A normal day with a phone leaves a trail: location from GPS, Wi-Fi and towers, time-stamped cell-site records, coordinates inside photos, advertising IDs in apps and cookies on websites.

cards.headline: You never posted where you went today. Your phone may know anyway.
cards.body: Nobody typed your route into anything. Yet an ordinary day with a phone leaves a trail of where you were and what you did. Follow one day, from breakfast to bedtime, and see which pieces get recorded.

cards.headline: Breakfast: the weather app asks where you are
cards.body: Your phone works out its location from GPS satellites, nearby Wi-Fi networks, cell towers and Bluetooth. An app has to ask before using it, and you can say yes only this once, or only while the app is open. Newer Android phones even let you hand over just your rough area instead of your exact spot. That little pop-up is the first fork in your data trail.

cards.headline: The commute: the towers keep a diary
cards.body: Your phone stays in touch with nearby cell sites all day, whatever the apps are doing. Each time it connects, the carrier's system logs a time-stamped record. In one 2018 US Supreme Court case, such records put a man's phone at 12,898 location points over 127 days, about 101 a day. You didn't share any of that. It's simply part of how a phone works.

cards.headline: Lunch, photos and browsing
cards.body: Snap a photo with location on and the camera embeds the spot's coordinates in the file itself, so they travel wherever the photo goes. Open an app and advertisers may follow you with your phone's unique advertising ID. Browse the web and sites can use cookies to recognize you even after you leave. Not one of these needed a post from you.

title: Metadata: The Envelope
objective: After this level you can explain why who, when and where you communicate can reveal as much as what you said.
summary: Metadata is data about data: for a call, the numbers, times and lengths but not the words. A Stanford study of 823 volunteers showed that pattern alone can reveal a heart condition.

cards.headline: You can learn a lot from an envelope without opening it.
cards.body: Picture a stack of envelopes addressed to one person over several months. You haven't read a single letter, yet you can see who wrote, to whom and when. Is that nothing? Or is it most of the story?

mascot.line: People mix these up: metadata isn't the message. It's everything about the message except the words.

cards.headline: Data about data
cards.body: That outside information has a name: metadata, meaning data about data. For a phone call it's the numbers, the time and how long you talked, but not a word you said. Files carry it too. A file's metadata describes things such as its format, which is how a program knows what kind of data is inside.

cards.headline: 823 volunteers and one heartbeat
cards.body: In a Stanford study published in 2016, researchers collected the call and text logs of 823 volunteers: numbers, times and lengths, no content. One person called a cardiology group, a pharmacy and a hotline for a heart-rhythm monitoring device. From that pattern alone, the researchers inferred the person likely had a cardiac arrhythmia. Nobody listened to a single call.

cards.headline: Why the envelope matters
cards.body: One call says little. Months of them reveal where someone goes, who they are close to and even highly sensitive traits. And locking the message itself doesn't hide the envelope: encryption leaves visible that two people are talking, and when, where and for how long. That's why metadata can matter as much as the words.

title: Why "Free" Apps Show Ads
objective: After this level you can connect the ad-funded business model to the data that apps and websites collect about you.
summary: Free services are often paid for by advertisers (about 98% of Meta's 2024 revenue), which rewards collecting data for targeted ads, often through ad companies' SDK code built into apps.

cards.headline: The app is free. Someone is still paying.
cards.body: You paid nothing for the app, yet someone pays for it to exist. For many free services, that someone is an advertiser. Follow the money and Level 62's data trail starts to make sense.

cards.fact: In 2024, advertising brought in about 98% of Meta's revenue.
cards.context: Its own results put ad revenue at $160.6 billion out of $164.5 billion in total. It's one clear example of the deal behind many free services: the people using it pay nothing, and the companies paying to reach them pay for almost everything.

cards.headline: Why the data matters to the deal
cards.body: Apps and websites can pick the ads you see from your browsing history or your location. A 2024 FTC staff report on nine large social media and video services found that many of their business models encouraged mass collection of user data to make money, especially through targeted ads. The staff saw that pull as in tension with users' privacy; two of the five commissioners filed partly dissenting statements.

cards.headline: Someone else's code inside your app
cards.body: Apps often show ads by building in a software development kit, or SDK: ready-made code from another company. Google's own disclosure for its mobile ads SDK says it automatically collects your phone's IP address (to estimate your general location), your taps and your advertising ID. Google Play makes app makers declare data their SDKs collect as part of the app's own disclosures.

title: Data Brokers
objective: After this level you can explain how companies you have never dealt with buy, combine and sell profiles of people.
summary: Data brokers gather details about people from records, purchases and browsing, combine them into profiles and segments (3,000 per person at one broker) and sell them, usually without people knowing.

cards.headline: Companies you've never heard of may have a file on you.
cards.body: You never signed up with them, bought from them or clicked their ads. Yet they may have your age range, your hobbies and guesses about your health. Meet the data brokers.

mascot.line: Keep this: each source knows a little. The broker's trick is putting the pieces together.

cards.headline: Buy, combine, sell
cards.body: Data brokers collect information about people from public records such as voter registrations, from purchase data, web browsing and warranty cards. They don't get it from you, so most people have no idea it's happening. Each source adds only a few details, but put together they form a detailed picture of a life, which brokers sell for uses like marketing and fraud checks.

cards.fact: One broker the FTC studied held 3,000 data segments for nearly every US consumer.
cards.context: The FTC looked closely at nine data brokers in 2014. A segment is a category a person is either placed in or not. Some sound harmless; others, like 'Expectant Parent', 'Diabetes Interest' and 'Cholesterol Focus', guess at sensitive matters such as health.

cards.headline: When the data is where you go
cards.body: Remember Level 62's location trail? In 2024 the FTC barred a broker, X-Mode Social, and its successor Outlogic from selling sensitive location data. The FTC alleged it had sold precise locations, gathered through its own apps and code built into other apps, that could reveal visits to medical clinics, places of worship and shelters. title: Anonymous Data That Isn't
objective: After this level you can explain how combining a few details, like ZIP code, birth date and sex, can put a name back on "anonymous" data.
summary: Sweeney re-identified 'anonymous' health data by matching ZIP code, birth date and sex to a voter list; those three details likely single out 87% of Americans, because details multiply.

cards.headline: The names were removed. A governor's medical record was found anyway.
cards.body: Massachusetts once collected health records for about 135,000 state employees and their families. The data was believed to be anonymous, so copies went to researchers and one was sold to industry. Then a computer scientist spent twenty dollars and put a name back.

cards.headline: Twenty dollars and a voter list
cards.body: Latanya Sweeney bought the voter list for Cambridge, Massachusetts. It held each voter's name, address, ZIP code, birth date and sex, and the health data still held ZIP code, birth date and sex. Governor William Weld's record was in the health data. Six Cambridge voters shared his birth date, only three were men, and only he lived in his ZIP code. One match, one name.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the 87%. Remember why: a few details multiply into more combinations than there are people.

cards.fact: Sweeney estimated that 87% of Americans were likely unique on ZIP code, birth date and sex alone.
cards.context: Why so few details? Because they multiply. In the Cambridge list, 2 sexes, 5 ZIP codes and birth dates across 365 days and 100 years gave 365,000 possible combinations, for only 54,805 voters. With far more combinations than people, most people sit alone in theirs.

cards.headline: Anonymous is a claim, not a switch
cards.body: The lesson: deleting names isn't the same as making data anonymous. The more details a dataset keeps about each person, the more likely they combine to point at one person, especially once someone links them to another dataset that has names attached. A voter list did it here; Level 65's brokers hold plenty more.

title: Data Breaches
objective: After this level you can explain what happens in a data breach, using Equifax in 2017, and connect it to the hashing and two-factor defenses.
summary: Equifax, 2017: an unpatched flaw let attackers in, unencrypted passwords opened 48 more databases, and data on 147 million people spilled. Hashing, a second factor and credit freezes help.

cards.headline: In 2017, one unpatched web page opened records on 147 million people.
cards.body: It wasn't a genius attack. A known flaw, a fix that never got installed, and a stash of passwords nobody had locked. Here's how the Equifax breach unfolded, and the defenses that make breaches like it less damaging.

events.label: A flaw in Apache Struts web software is announced; one portal misses the fix

cards.headline: The passwords nobody locked
cards.body: Inside the portal, the attackers found usernames and passwords stored unencrypted. Those let them reach 48 more databases beyond the portal's 3. They took names, dates of birth and Social Security numbers, sending the data out in small encrypted pieces that looked like normal traffic.

cards.headline: Defenses that shrink the damage
cards.body: NIST's guidelines require services to store passwords only salted and hashed, scrambled one way so a stolen copy can't simply be read back. With multi-factor authentication, a thief holding your password still can't meet the second requirement. And for you in the US, a credit freeze is free and stops new credit being opened in your name.

title: End-to-End Encryption
objective: After this level you can explain why end-to-end encryption means even the service can't read your messages, and why governments debate it.
summary: With end-to-end encryption only sender and recipient hold the keys. Officials call it warrant-proof; security experts say any built-in door adds a weakness.

cards.headline: Some messaging services can't read your messages, even if they wanted to.
cards.body: Not because they promise not to peek, but because they never hold the key. That design is why law enforcement officials and security experts argue about it.

cards.headline: Two ways to lock a message

items.label: Encrypted in transit
points: Locked from your phone to the service's servers, then on to your friend
The service can see unencrypted copies in the middle

items.label: End-to-end encrypted
points: Locked by the sender, unlocked only by the recipient
Only the two ends hold the keys; the service can't read it

cards.headline: The key is just bits
cards.body: An encryption key is a string of bits. The widely used AES standard offers keys 128, 192 or 256 bits long. Each added bit of key doubles the number of possible keys, so every extra bit doubles the guessing an attacker would face. But remember Level 63: even end-to-end encryption leaves visible who is talking, and when and for how long.

mascot.line: This is a debate with named sides. Your job here is to understand both arguments, not to pick a winner.

cards.headline: The lawful access debate
cards.body: Law enforcement officials call strong end-to-end encryption 'warrant-proof': a company without the keys can't decrypt messages even for a search warrant. Security experts answer that any built-in door that a key can open, whoever holds the key, adds a weakness criminals could exploit too. As of a January 2024 congressional research report, no one had shown how to build a door that opens only for lawful use.

title: Privacy Laws
objective: After this level you can explain what laws like the EU's GDPR and California's privacy law let you ask of companies that hold your data.
summary: The GDPR lets you see, correct, erase and move your data, answered within a month; California's law gives rights to know, delete, correct, limit and opt out.

cards.headline: You can ask a company: what do you know about me?
cards.body: In many places, that question isn't just polite. It's a legal right, with a deadline for the answer. Two laws show what you can ask for: Europe's GDPR and California's privacy law.

cards.headline: Europe's GDPR
cards.body: The EU's General Data Protection Regulation has applied since 25 May 2018. It lets you get a copy of the personal data a company holds on you, have wrong data corrected and, in many cases, have it erased. The company must answer within one month. The most serious breaches of the rules can bring fines of up to 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide yearly turnover, whichever is higher.

cards.headline: Take your data with you
cards.body: The GDPR also gives a right to data portability: you can receive the data you gave a company in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format, and pass it to another service. Britain's data regulator, the ICO, names CSV, a standard format for spreadsheet data, as one that qualifies. A file is only useful if the next program knows how to read it.

cards.headline: California's version
cards.body: California's Consumer Privacy Act took effect in 2020, and amendments expanding it began on January 1, 2023. Residents can ask a business what it has collected about them, have it deleted or corrected, limit use of sensitive information, and tell it to stop selling or sharing their data. Businesses must answer requests to know, delete or correct within 45 calendar days.

cards.body: Chapter 7 finale. At breakfast you let a weather app see your location. Follow that single piece of data through everything this chapter covered, and find where the brakes are.

cards.headline: Out of your phone and into a profile
cards.body: The location comes from GPS, Wi-Fi and cell towers. If the app shows ads, an ad company's SDK inside it may collect your advertising ID too. Brokers combine pieces like these into profiles, and use websites with sign-ups and cookies to match what you do offline to the ads you see online. Strip off your name and the trail can still point to you, because a few details combine into a pattern only you fit.

cards.headline: Stored somewhere, and the brakes
cards.body: Somewhere your ping becomes a row in a database table. If that company is breached, as Equifax was in 2017, anything stored carelessly, like Equifax's unencrypted passwords, can unlock the rest. The brakes: passwords kept only as salted hashes, a second factor, encryption that hides what you say (though not the metadata), and laws like the GDPR and California's that let you see, correct and delete what's held on you.

title: How Maps Find the Fastest Route
objective: After this level you can explain how a route-finding algorithm explores a road network step by step and uses live traffic to update it.
summary: A map becomes a weighted graph; Dijkstra's 1956 method grows outward from the start, closest place first, and live traffic keeps changing the weights.

cards.headline: In 1956, a programmer solved your drive home over a cup of coffee.
cards.body: Finding the quickest way from here to there is the puzzle your map app solves every time you ask for directions. Edsger Dijkstra cracked it in about twenty minutes on a café terrace in Amsterdam. His trick starts by seeing a map not as a picture, but as dots and lines.

cards.headline: A map made of dots and lines
cards.body: To a computer, a road map is a weighted graph. Each intersection is a dot, called a node. Each road between two intersections is a line, called an edge. And each edge carries a weight: the cost of travelling it, such as minutes of driving. The best route is simply the path whose weights add up to the smallest total. Fewest turns doesn't count. Smallest sum wins.

mascot.line: Keep this: always expand the closest unfinished place next. That one rule, repeated, is the whole algorithm.

cards.headline: Always grow from the closest place
cards.body: Start at your front door, at distance 0. Note how far each neighboring intersection is. Now take the unvisited place with the smallest known distance, check its neighbors, and lower any distance you can beat. Then repeat. The search spreads outward like a ripple, nearest places first, until your destination is the one picked next. At that moment, its distance is the shortest there is.

cards.headline: Weights that change by the minute
cards.body: Dijkstra's 1956 map had fixed distances. A map app keeps changing its weights. Google Maps, for example, uses aggregate location data from people navigating to see current traffic, and blends it with each road's historical patterns to predict traffic later in your drive. If it predicts a jam ahead, it automatically finds a lower-traffic alternative. A route search is only as good as the numbers it adds up.

title: "Because You Watched"
objective: After this level you can explain how recommendation systems suggest things by finding people whose tastes match yours.
summary: Collaborative filtering suggests what people with overlapping tastes liked; the Netflix Prize paid $1 million for better guesses, and brand-new items start cold.

cards.headline: In 2006, Netflix offered $1 million for better guesses about your taste.
cards.body: The money would go to anyone who could make its recommendations 10 percent more accurate. Why pay so much to guess what you'll watch next? Because guessing well is the whole trick behind "Because you watched."

cards.headline: People like you
cards.body: Most recommendations rest on a simple idea: if two people enjoyed the same things, they're likely to share other favorites too. Collaborative filtering puts that to work. It compares your ratings and choices with everyone else's, and when someone whose taste overlaps with yours loved something you haven't tried, it suggests it to you. The system needs no idea what the film is about. It only needs the overlap.

cards.headline: A million-dollar tie
cards.body: Netflix's raw material was star ratings, from one to five, that customers gave movies. Contestants used them to predict how people would rate films they hadn't rated yet. In September 2009 the prize went to BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos, itself a merger of teams. The finish was so close that its final entry and the runner-up's were a mathematical tie. The team that submitted first took the million.

cards.headline: Someone has to go first
cards.body: Collaborative filtering has a blind spot. A brand-new film that nobody has watched or rated overlaps with no one, so the system has nothing to learn it from. This is called the cold-start problem. The newest thing in the catalog can be the hardest one to recommend, until enough people find it some other way.

title: How Your Feed Is Ranked
objective: After this level you can explain how social feeds score posts by predicted engagement instead of showing them in time order.
summary: Instagram switched from newest-first to ranked in 2016; feeds gather posts, read signals, predict your reactions and sort by the combined score.

cards.headline: By 2016, Instagram users were missing 70% of the posts in their feeds.
cards.body: When Instagram launched in 2010, the feed was one stream of photos in time order. As more people shared more, nobody could keep up. So the app stopped asking "what's newest?" and started asking "what will you care about?"

cards.headline: From newest first to a score
cards.body: In 2016 Instagram introduced a ranked feed. Facebook describes its own ranking as a pipeline. First, gather the inventory: every post you could see right now. Next, check signals, clues such as your history of interacting with the person who posted. Then make predictions about each post. Finally, combine them into a relevance score and put the posts in order. Facebook says it weighs thousands of signals.

cards.headline: A leaderboard of predicted reactions
cards.body: The predictions are about engagement: what you're likely to do with a post. Instagram says the five it watches most closely in Feed are how likely you are to spend a few seconds on a post, comment on it, like it, reshare it and tap the poster's profile photo. The more likely an action, and the more weight it carries, the higher the post climbs. Your feed is a ranking of guesses about you.

cards.headline: Time order didn't vanish
cards.body: Ranking became the default, not the only option. Facebook's Feeds tab, launched in 2022, shows the newest posts first, in reverse chronological order. Same pile of posts, two ways to sort it: by when they were posted, or by how you're predicted to react.

title: The Auction Behind Every Ad
objective: After this level you can explain how an ad space is auctioned in a fraction of a second while a page loads, using data about you.
summary: While a page loads, a bid request describing you goes out, bidders reply within a deadline of milliseconds, the highest bid wins, and regulators have questioned the data it carries.

cards.headline: Before this page finished loading, the ad space on it may have been sold.
cards.body: Between your tap and the finished page, companies can bid to show you an ad, and one of them wins. The whole sale happens in milliseconds. So what do the bidders know about you, and how do they decide so fast?

cards.headline: The bid request
cards.body: As a site loads, its publisher (the site's owner) can put an ad space up for auction. A message called a bid request goes out to would-be advertisers. According to the UK's data protection regulator, the ICO, bid requests commonly include your IP address, cookie IDs (codes stored by your browser), your browser and device type, your location, time zone and language. Bidders read those details and decide what showing you an ad is worth.

mascot.line: Don't memorize 80 or 1,000. Remember the shape: a request goes out, bids come back, the highest one in time wins.

cards.fact: On Google's ad exchange, a bidder typically gets 80 to 1,000 milliseconds to reply.
cards.context: Replies that arrive late are simply left out. The rest enter the auction, the highest bid wins the space, and that ad appears on your page. Billions of online ads are placed this way every day.

cards.headline: Why a regulator looked closely
cards.body: A bid request can reach many companies at once. In 2019 the ICO reported that bid requests normally contain personal data, and that many companies taking part in real-time bidding were doing so without fully understanding the privacy issues involved. That's the tension at the heart of the auction: the details that help bidders judge what an ad is worth are details about you.

title: How Spam Filters Learn
objective: After this level you can explain how a spam filter learns from labeled examples which words and signals predict junk mail.
summary: Graham's 2002 filter counted words in a spam pile and a good-mail pile; labeled examples teach it, and every Report spam click keeps it learning as spam evolves.

cards.headline: One of the best spam clues Paul Graham ever found was "ff0000".
cards.body: It's the web code for bright red. In 2002 his filter found it about as telling as any rude word. He never told the filter to look for red. It found that clue on its own, from examples.

cards.headline: Two piles and a lot of counting
cards.body: Graham's essay "A Plan for Spam" laid out the method. Start with one pile of known spam and one pile of good mail. Count how often every word appears in each pile. A word common in spam but rare in good mail gets a high spam probability; your best friend's name gets a low one. A new email is scored by combining the probabilities of its most telling words.

cards.headline: The labels do the teaching
cards.body: Each email in those piles comes labeled: spam or not spam. The filter works out which features predict the label. Machine learning people call this supervised learning, training on labeled examples, and spotting spam is one of its standard examples. The piles are the teacher.

cards.headline: Your clicks keep it learning
cards.body: Graham argued everyone should have two delete buttons: ordinary delete and delete-as-spam, so each person's piles keep growing from their own mail. Gmail's Report spam button feeds the same kind of learning: Google says that as you report more spam, Gmail identifies similar emails as spam more efficiently. That matters because spam keeps changing, and a filter that learns from new examples changes with it.

title: Matching Riders and Drivers
objective: After this level you can explain how ride and delivery apps match each request to a nearby driver and raise prices when demand spikes.
summary: Closest isn't always quickest, so ride apps match riders and drivers in batches to cut average waits; when requests outnumber drivers, surge prices rise, within legal limits.

cards.headline: Why doesn't a ride app just send the closest car?
cards.body: It used to. Uber says it first matched riders by asking "Who's closest?" and learned that closest doesn't always mean quickest. Traffic, an overpass or a river can turn a car that looks near into a long wait.

cards.headline: Matching in batches
cards.body: Now, in the seconds after you request a ride, Uber looks at nearby drivers and riders together, as one batch. Then it pairs them up to cut the average wait for everyone, not just to hand each rider the closest car. Picture two riders on the same street: giving the first one the nearest car might leave the second waiting ages. Sorting out all the pairs at once can do better for both.

cards.headline: When requests outnumber cars
cards.body: Bad weather, rush hour and big events can bring more ride requests to an area than there are drivers. That's when surge pricing switches on. Prices rise, updated in real time and different from one neighborhood to the next. The higher price is meant to pull more drivers toward the busy area, while some riders choose to wait for prices to drop. The price becomes a signal that moves cars.

cards.headline: A limit on the surge
cards.body: Surge pricing also has limits set outside the app. In July 2014 Uber agreed with New York's attorney general to cap its prices during emergencies and natural disasters, in line with the state's price-gouging law, and the rules applied nationally.

title: Moderating Billions of Posts
objective: After this level you can explain how platforms combine automated filters and human reviewers, and why both make mistakes at scale.
summary: Fingerprints catch copies of known illegal images, machines flag new posts for human reviewers, and at millions of removals a day even a small error rate means many wrong calls.

cards.headline: Meta thinks 1 or 2 in 10 of its removals may have been mistakes.
cards.body: Meta removed millions of pieces of content a day in December 2024, and published that estimate of its own errors in January 2025. To see how a system ends up wrong that often, look at the jobs it has to do: catching copies, judging new posts, and doing both at enormous scale.

cards.headline: Catching copies with fingerprints
cards.body: The clearest case is an image already known to be illegal. In 2009 Microsoft and Dartmouth College developed PhotoDNA. It computes a digital signature, a kind of fingerprint called a hash, from an image, then compares it with the signatures of images already identified as illegal. A match flags a copy. The catch: it can only find images someone has identified before.

cards.headline: Machines flag, people judge
cards.body: Brand-new posts need judgment. Meta says its technology detects most violating content before anyone reports it, and sends potentially violating posts to review teams, thousands of reviewers around the world, to check and act on. Context is the hard part. The same words can be a slur in one post and mean something else entirely in another.

cards.headline: Why mistakes pile up
cards.body: In September 2016 Facebook removed posts of "The Terror of War", the Vietnam War photo of a naked girl fleeing a napalm attack. After a global outcry, it reinstated the photo, citing its history and global importance. A rule that fits almost every case still misfires on some. At millions of removals a day, even a small share of wrong calls adds up to a lot of them.

title: Feedback Loops
objective: After this level you can explain how a recommendation can shape the very behavior it later learns from.
summary: In a music experiment published in 2006, visible download counts made hits unequal and unpredictable; recommenders face the same loop because they learn from clicks they helped cause.

cards.headline: What if the hits were partly luck?
cards.body: In 2004 three Columbia University researchers built their own music site to test that. They let the same songs compete in eight separate worlds and watched which ones became hits. The answer matters for any system that learns from what people click.

cards.headline: Eight worlds, different hits
cards.body: Salganik, Dodds and Watts offered listeners songs by unknown bands. In each of eight social worlds, people could see how often every song had been downloaded in their own world; another group couldn't see counts at all. Showing popularity made success more unequal and harder to predict. The best songs rarely did badly and the worst rarely did well, but anything in between could happen.

cards.headline: The loop inside a recommender
cards.body: A recommender runs a similar loop automatically. It shows you items, you click some, and those clicks become its next lesson. But it is usually trained on data from people who were already shown its recommendations. So it can't easily tell whether you picked something because you liked it or because it was put in front of you. Researchers call this a feedback loop.

mascot.line: This ties the chapter together: recommendations and ranked feeds both learn from clicks they helped cause.

cards.headline: Where the loop leads
cards.body: Recommenders tend to show a few popular items often while most items get ignored, and the loop of recommending, reacting and retraining can amplify that popularity bias. Simulations by Chaney and colleagues found it can make people's behavior more alike without making them any better off. The system ends up shaping the very data it learns from.

title: Who Checks the Algorithm?
objective: After this level you can explain how audits, explanations and appeal rights let people test and challenge automated decisions.
summary: Auditors test systems from outside, as the 2018 Gender Shades audit did; the GDPR can give rights to a human, to contest and to information, and New York City requires hiring-tool bias audits.

cards.headline: How do you test a system whose code you can't see?
cards.body: Most algorithms that choose for you are private. Yet researchers have found ways to check them from the outside, and some laws now give people rights when a machine alone makes a significant decision about them.

cards.headline: Testing from outside
cards.body: An audit asks whether a system behaves the way it should. If the code is public, auditors can read it. If not, they test from outside: send it repeated queries and watch what comes back, or run programmed fake users, called sock puppets, and compare how the system treats them. You learn what a box does by choosing its inputs and watching its outputs.

cards.fact: In 2018, Gender Shades found error rates up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women and at most 0.8% for lighter-skinned men.
cards.context: Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested three commercial gender classification products on a benchmark of 1,270 faces, balanced by gender and skin type. They sent in faces and compared the answers across groups. The gaps showed up only because someone chose the inputs carefully.

cards.headline: A right to a human
cards.body: In the EU, the GDPR gives people the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing when it has legal or similarly significant effects on them. Where such decisions are allowed because they are needed for a contract or the person agreed, people keep at least the right to human intervention, to give their point of view and to contest the decision. They can also ask for meaningful information about the logic involved.

cards.headline: Audits by law
cards.body: New York City went further for hiring. Its Local Law 144 of 2021 bars employers from using an automated hiring tool unless it has had a bias audit within one year before use, a summary of the results is public and candidates are told. Enforcement began on July 5, 2023.

title: Rules or Examples?
objective: After this level you can decide whether a task is better solved by writing rules or by learning from examples, and say why.
summary: Arthur Samuel's checkers program learned from its games. Rules work when you can state them exactly; examples win when the patterns are too many to write down.

cards.headline: The checkers program that learned to play better than its author
cards.body: At IBM, Arthur Samuel wrote a checkers program that recorded each position it saw and whether it led to a win or a loss, then used those records in later games. It got better the more it played. Samuel called this machine learning, a term he coined, and in 1959 he reported that a computer could learn to play better checkers than the person who wrote the program.

cards.headline: Two ways to get a job done
cards.body: The classic way is rules. A person writes every step, often as yes-or-no tests like Level 6's gates: water the garden if the soil is dry AND it is NOT raining. Machine learning flips this around. You train software, called a model, on examples, and its logic is learned from the data instead of written as explicit rules. Rules come out of a programmer's head; a model's patterns come out of its examples.

cards.headline: When rules run out
cards.body: Rules work when you can say exactly what matters. Now try writing rules for reading a stranger's handwriting: every loop, slant and smudge. IBM puts the problem plainly: as tasks get more complex, rule-based systems become brittle, because it's often impossible to write down every pattern and variable that matters. That's where learning from examples earns its keep.

cards.headline: When rules win
cards.body: Examples come at a price. Machine learning requires data, and a model needs looking after for as long as it runs. So Google's own machine learning guides advise not being afraid to launch without it: check for a non-ML solution first, because that becomes the benchmark any model has to beat. If you can state the rule exactly, like a sales tax rate, write the rule.

title: Training and Testing
objective: After this level you can judge a model by how it does on data it never saw, and spot overfitting when it only memorized its training set.
summary: A model is judged on a test set it never saw. Overfitting is memorizing the training set: low training error, high test error, like a suit pinned to one mannequin.

cards.headline: A suit pinned to one mannequin fits exactly one mannequin.
cards.body: A tailor could fit a suit to every bump of a shop dummy and still make something no real customer can wear. Machine learning has the same trap. The way to catch it is simple, and it's the whole idea of this level: test on examples the model has never seen.

cards.headline: Three piles of examples
cards.body: Before training, the data is split. The training set is what the model learns from. A validation set checks progress during training. The test set is held back to judge the finished model. Google's course is strict about it: delete any test example that duplicates a training example, because the only fair test is on new examples. Otherwise it's an exam with the answers leaked.

mascot.line: People mix these up: a great score on training data shows memory. Only the test score shows learning.

cards.headline: Memorized, not learned
cards.body: A model can match its training set so closely that it fails on new data. That's overfitting: the suit that fits only the dummy. The telltale sign is a low error rate on the training data next to a high error rate on the test data. A model that makes good predictions on new data generalizes well, and generalizing is the whole point.

cards.fact: A 20-pixel black-and-white picture has 1,048,576 possible patterns.
cards.context: That's Level 2's doubling: if each pixel is one bit, every added pixel doubles the count, and 2 to the 20th is 1,048,576. A photo from a 24-megapixel camera has about 24 million pixels, each color set by a number from 0 to 255. So nearly every picture a model meets after training is one it has never seen.

title: Inside a Neural Network
objective: After this level you can explain how a neural network learns by nudging millions of weights, a little at a time, to shrink its errors.
summary: Neurons in layers multiply inputs by weights and add them up. Training measures the loss and backpropagation nudges every weight a little to shrink it, again and again.

cards.headline: A neural network is mostly multiplying and adding. A lot of it.
cards.body: The name suggests a brain in a box. Inside, it's stranger and simpler: layers of small calculators, each doing sums with adjustable numbers called weights. Training nudges those numbers, a small amount at a time, until the answers come out right.

cards.headline: Neurons: multiply, add, pass it on
cards.body: A neural network stacks simple artificial neurons in layers: an input layer takes in the data, hidden layers in the middle recombine it, and an output layer gives the prediction. Each neuron multiplies every input by its own weight, adds up the results, adds one more number called the bias, and passes the total on. A big weight means that input counts for a lot.

cards.headline: Learning is nudging
cards.body: After a guess, training calculates the loss: how wrong the prediction was. Backpropagation then works backward through the network, calculating how much each weight and bias contributed to the error. Every weight moves a small amount in the direction that shrinks the loss. Then the loop repeats: guess, measure, nudge, again and again.

cards.fact: GPT-3, a 2020 language model, had 175 billion parameters.
cards.context: Parameters are the weights and biases, and each one was tuned by the same loop. The recipe is older than it looks: in 1986, David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams described in Nature how to train a network by back-propagating its errors and adjusting its weights.

title: Why AI Needs So Many Chips
objective: After this level you can explain why training large models takes thousands of graphics chips and large amounts of electricity.
summary: GPUs, built for 3-D graphics, run thousands of calculations at once. GPT-3 needed 10,000 of them for about 15 days and an estimated 1,287 MWh (2021 estimate).

cards.headline: The chips that train AI were built to draw 3-D graphics.
cards.body: Graphics processing units, or GPUs, were designed to speed up 3-D graphics. Today they train neural networks. Why would a chip made for pictures be the right tool for learning? Because deep learning is a mountain of calculations that a GPU can run thousands at a time.

cards.headline: Thousands of workers at once
cards.body: Level 8's processor races through instructions largely one after another: CPUs generally work serially, finishing one process before the next. A GPU spreads the work over hundreds or even thousands of cores, all calculating at the same moment. Deep learning is mostly huge grids of multiplications, like Level 83's neurons, so for training a GPU is far more efficient than a traditional processor.

cards.fact: A 2021 study estimated that training GPT-3 kept 10,000 GPUs busy for about 15 days.
cards.context: That's 148,000 chip-days: about 400 years of work for a single chip. Splitting the job across thousands of chips turns centuries into weeks. And the clusters keep growing: in 2024, Meta reported training its largest Llama 3 model on up to 16,000 GPUs.

cards.headline: The electricity bill
cards.body: Thousands of chips running for weeks draw serious power. A 2021 study estimated that training GPT-3 used 1,287 megawatt-hours of electricity. That's about what 120 average US homes used in a year in 2022. And it's one training run of one model, as estimated in 2021.

title: Tokens and the Next Word
objective: After this level you can explain how a large language model splits text into tokens and writes by predicting one token after another.
summary: Text is chopped into subword tokens, each swapped for a number. The model scores every token in its vocabulary, one is picked and appended, and the loop repeats.

cards.headline: A chatbot may never see the word "annoyingly" whole.
cards.body: Before a language model reads your message, the text is chopped into pieces, and every piece is swapped for a number. You met tokens in Everyday Technology. Here's what actually happens to your words on the way in, and how a reply comes out.

cards.headline: Chopping text into tokens
cards.body: Most language models use subword tokens. Frequent words stay whole, while rare words are split into meaningful pieces that turn up more often: "annoyingly" becomes "annoying" plus "ly". That way a fixed list of pieces can still cover words the model rarely met, and the meaning survives in the parts.

cards.headline: Every token gets a number
cards.body: Models can only process numbers, so the tokenizer swaps each token for its ID: its number in the model's vocabulary. GPT-2, from 2019, had a vocabulary of 50,257 tokens. It's Level 4's idea one size up. Unicode gives a number to every character; a tokenizer gives a number to every chunk.

mascot.line: Keep this: a chatbot never picks a whole answer. It picks one token, then starts again with that token added.

cards.headline: One token, then again
cards.body: To write, the model gives a score to every token in its vocabulary, and one is picked. That token is added to the text, and the whole thing goes back in for the next pick, so each new token depends on all the ones before it. A setting called temperature shapes the pick: higher is more random, lower more focused and predictable.
