title: From Predictor to Assistant
objective: After this level you can explain how pretraining on vast amounts of text, then fine-tuning with human feedback, turns a text predictor into a chatbot.
summary: Next-token prediction isn't instruction-following. Fine-tuning on human-written answers, then RLHF with a reward model trained on rankings, turns a predictor into an assistant.

cards.headline: Trained on the internet, a model learns to continue text, not to help.
cards.body: A model pretrained on vast amounts of text is very good at one thing: predicting the next token. But predicting what comes next on a web page is a different goal from following your instructions helpfully and safely, as a 2022 paper pointed out. Turning one into the other took people.

cards.headline: Step 1: show it good answers
cards.body: Pretraining gives the model its raw skill with language. Then people write example answers to real prompts, showing the behavior they want, and the model is fine-tuned on those demonstrations. It's the same nudging of weights as Level 83, now aimed at answering like a helpful assistant instead of continuing a web page.

cards.headline: Step 2: rank, reward, repeat
cards.body: Writing perfect answers is slow, so labelers do something quicker: they rank several of the model's answers from best to worst. A second model, the reward model, learns from those rankings to score any answer by how much people would likely prefer it. The chatbot is then tuned to earn higher scores. That's reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF.

cards.fact: A tuned model with 100 times fewer parameters beat the untuned giant.
cards.context: In the 2022 tests, people preferred answers from a 1.3 billion-parameter tuned model to those of the 175 billion-parameter GPT-3. The authors added a caveat: the labelers were a team of 40 contractors, so the model was aligned to a specific group, not to any broader notion of human values.

title: Why Chatbots Make Things Up
objective: After this level you can explain why a language model can state false things fluently, and check a chatbot's answer against a source.
summary: A language model writes likely text, so it can confabulate: state falsehoods confidently, even fake citations. The check that works is a source outside the chatbot.

cards.headline: A lawyer asked the chatbot: is this case real? It said yes.
cards.body: In the 2023 Mata v. Avianca case, lawyers filed a brief citing court cases that ChatGPT had made up. One lawyer asked ChatGPT whether a case was real, and it said the case existed. It didn't. Why would a machine vouch for something it invented?

cards.headline: Likely is not the same as true
cards.body: NIST's name for this is confabulation: confidently stated but false content, often called hallucinations. It's a natural result of how these models work: they produce text that fits the statistical patterns of their training data, one likely token after another. Level 7's adder gets 1 + 1 = 10 by fixed rules. Picking a likely next token follows no such rule for truth.

cards.headline: Why guess instead of saying "I don't know"?
cards.body: A 2025 research paper offered one explanation. Like students facing a hard exam, models guess when they're unsure, because training and most evaluations reward guessing over admitting uncertainty. On a test graded only right or wrong, a blank scores nothing and a guess sometimes scores. So a confident wrong answer can look better on paper than an honest "I don't know."

mascot.line: Keep this: a chatbot checking itself isn't a check. The source has to exist outside it.

cards.headline: Check outside the chatbot
cards.body: NIST warns that these models can produce made-up citations that appear to back up an answer. So asking the chatbot "are you sure?" just asks the same guesser again. The check that works is outside it: find the source yourself and see that it exists and says what was claimed. The lawyer did search a free site for the case. He couldn't find it, and cited it anyway.

title: Pictures From Noise
objective: After this level you can explain how image generators learn to turn random noise, step by step, into a picture that matches a prompt.
summary: Diffusion models learn to remove noise added step by step to real images, then generate by denoising fresh random static, steered by a text prompt.

cards.headline: Many AI pictures start as static.
cards.body: Ask a diffusion image generator, the kind behind many popular tools, for a lighthouse at dusk and it doesn't sketch or paint. It starts from random noise and removes noise, step by step, until a lighthouse is left. The clever part is how it learned to clean.

cards.headline: Training: ruin pictures on purpose
cards.body: To train a diffusion model, real images are turned into pure noise by adding a little noise at each step. The model's job is to run the film backward. At each step it predicts the noise in the image and removes a fraction of it. Ruining pictures is easy; learning to undo the ruin is the whole skill.

cards.headline: Generating: from noise to lighthouse
cards.body: To make something new, a trained diffusion model starts from fresh random noise and removes noise step by step. A text prompt, interpreted by a separate language model, steers the result toward what you asked for. The influential 2020 paper by Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel at UC Berkeley used 1,000 steps.

cards.headline: Noise, in numbers
cards.body: Remember Level 5: each pixel's color is three numbers, red, green and blue, from 0 to 255. Add random noise to those numbers, step after step, and the picture ends up looking like TV static. Generating runs that the other way: the model changes the pixel numbers a little at each step until they form a picture.

title: Deepfakes and Proving What's Real
objective: After this level you can weigh the ways to tell a real photo, video or voice from a synthetic one, including provenance labels.
summary: People spot AI faces at about chance (48%) and detectors chase generators. Provenance, like C2PA Content Credentials, can be signed, but metadata is often stripped.

cards.headline: Real face or AI face? People scored 48%.
cards.body: In a 2022 study, people sorting real faces from AI-made ones were right 48% of the time, close to the 50% of pure chance. Training raised that only to 59%. So if your eyes can't settle it, what can?

mascot.line: This is Level 82 again: a detector that only knows its training generators hasn't learned to generalize.

cards.headline: Detectors: a race with no finish line
cards.body: Software detectors hunt for traces that generators leave behind. NIST describes it as a cat-and-mouse game: as new detection methods appear, generators improve and learn to slip past them. And detectors often work best only on the generators they were trained on, while fakes from newer generators keep arriving.

cards.headline: Ask where it came from, not how it looks
cards.body: Provenance flips the question. The C2PA, a coalition of companies and organizations, publishes an open standard that records a file's origin and edits, shown to people as Content Credentials: a sort of nutrition label for media. The record can carry a digital signature, which gives assurance of who signed it and that nothing changed after signing.

cards.headline: What a missing label means
cards.body: The weak spot: metadata can be stripped from a file, and often is when files are shared on social media, sometimes to deceive and sometimes for privacy. So a label that checks out is real evidence, but a missing label proves little either way. As Level 10 showed, context decides what bits mean, and a photo's pixels don't say who made them.

title: Megabits, Megabytes and Speed
objective: After this level you can work out a real download time from an advertised internet speed, and spot claims that mix up bits and bytes.
summary: Speeds are sold in megabits per second, files in megabytes. Divide by 8: a 100 Mbps line moves at most 12.5 MB a second, and typical speeds are lower.

cards.headline: Your plan says 100. Your download says 12.5. Nobody is lying.
cards.body: A 100 Mbps plan, a download bar showing about 12.5 MB a second. It looks like a rip-off. It's really a capital letter. Level 2's bits and bytes are hiding in the units.

mascot.line: People mix these up all the time. Small b is bits, big B is bytes, and it takes 8 bits to make a byte.

cards.headline: Little b, big B
cards.body: Internet speeds are sold in megabits per second, written Mbps with a small b. File sizes are counted in megabytes, MB, with a capital B. And a byte, as Level 2 showed, is 8 bits. So one megabyte per second equals 8 megabits per second. To turn a speed into file terms, divide it by 8. The ad isn't wrong. It just counts in smaller pieces.

cards.fact: A 100 Mbps line moves at most about 12.5 megabytes a second.
cards.context: So a 1 GB file, about 1,000 MB, needs at least 80 seconds, and a 100 MB game at least 8. The recipe works for any plan: divide the speed by 8, then divide the file size by the answer. Notice the words 'at most' and 'at least'. This is the best case.

cards.headline: Up to, and typical
cards.body: The number in the ad is a ceiling. Since April 2024, large US internet providers have had to publish a broadband label listing typical download and upload speeds at peak hours for each plan they sell. So your worked-out download time is the fastest it could go. Redo the sum with the typical speed and you'll know what to expect on a busy evening, when everyone else is streaming too.

title: Is My Phone Listening to Me?
objective: After this level you can weigh the evidence on whether phones secretly record conversations for ads, and the simpler explanations for eerie ads.
summary: A 2018 test of 17,000+ Android apps found none secretly sending audio, but found apps sending screen recordings. Location, browsing and app data explain eerie ads.

cards.headline: You mention hiking boots. An hour later, a boot ad.
cards.body: It feels like proof that your phone is listening. Some researchers decided to test it instead of guessing. What they found is less spooky than the rumor, and in one way more surprising.

cards.headline: The test: 17,000 apps
cards.body: In a 2018 study, Northeastern University researchers ran more than 17,000 popular Android apps with an automated test program and watched what each one sent out. They were looking for the microphone switching on and audio leaving the phone. They found no app doing it. That's strong evidence, not proof: it covered the Android apps they could test, not every app on every phone.

cards.headline: What they found instead
cards.body: The surprise was the screen. Some apps sent screenshots and screen recordings to other companies without telling the user. One food-delivery app sent its screens to an analytics firm. So the leak the study actually found wasn't your voice. It was whatever happened to be on your screen.

cards.headline: The boring explanation
cards.body: Ads don't need your voice. Your phone's GPS and nearby cell towers reveal where you go, tracking pixels on websites record what you browse and put in your cart, and companies combine data from many apps into one profile. That's usually enough to guess at hiking boots. And you can check the microphone yourself: on an iPhone with iOS 14 or later, an orange dot appears when an app is using it, and a green dot when the camera is on too.

title: What AI Can and Can't Do in 2026
objective: After this level you can judge a claim about AI against what current systems reliably do and where they still fail.
summary: AI in 2026 wins olympiad gold yet reads clocks at 50.1%: a jagged frontier. NIST warns of confident falsehoods. Judge any claim by task, date and a source check.

cards.headline: Gold at the math olympiad. A coin flip on a clock.
cards.body: In 2025, AI systems reached gold-medal scores at the International Mathematical Olympiad. Yet in the 2026 AI Index, the best model read an analog clock right only 50.1% of the time. So when someone says AI can or can't do something, the honest reply is: which task, and when was it checked?

cards.headline: A jagged frontier
cards.body: Researchers call this uneven shape AI's jagged frontier. Picture a coastline rather than a wall: the edge reaches far out on some tasks, like olympiad math, and cuts deep inland on others, like telling the time from a clock face. Brilliance at one task tells you surprisingly little about the task next door. So judge a claim task by task, never by the system's best trick.

cards.headline: Fluent isn't the same as right
cards.body: There's a second catch. In 2024 NIST, the US standards agency, listed confabulation as a risk of generative AI: content stated confidently that is simply false, often called hallucination. A wrong answer arrives in the same smooth, sure voice as a right one. So the tone of an answer is no evidence at all. For anything that matters, check it against a source.

cards.headline: Date every claim
cards.body: Abilities also move fast. On one leading coding benchmark, the top AI score rose from about 60% to near 100% in a single year, the 2026 AI Index reports. So 'AI can't do X' may be out of date by next spring, and 'AI can do X' may mean X on a test, not on your problem. Ask which task, when it was measured, and whether it's the kind of task where AI is known to stumble.

title: Will Quantum Break Encryption?
objective: After this level you can explain which kinds of encryption a large quantum computer could break, and how post-quantum standards prepare for it.
summary: A large quantum computer could break public-key encryption like RSA, not strong symmetric keys like AES. NIST released post-quantum standards in August 2024.

cards.headline: 'Quantum computers will break all encryption.' Half right.
cards.body: A big enough quantum computer would break some of the locks that guard the internet, but not all of them. Knowing which ones is the whole story, and the fix is already being rolled out.

cards.headline: The locks at risk
cards.body: In 1994 Peter Shor devised an algorithm that would let a large enough quantum computer factor huge numbers, breaking encryption built on multiplying two large primes. Much public-key encryption, the kind strangers use to set up a shared secret, rests on problems like that. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says such a machine would break today's public-key methods, including RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography.

mascot.line: Keep this: quantum threatens public-key encryption, not all encryption. Headlines skip that difference.

cards.headline: The locks that hold
cards.body: Symmetric encryption, where both sides already share one secret key, is a different story. The NCSC says quantum computers don't significantly affect it: methods such as AES with keys of at least 128 bits can still be used. The real worry is timing. Someone could record encrypted data today and store it, planning to unlock it once a quantum computer exists. Secrets that must stay secret for decades are the ones at risk now.

cards.headline: New locks, already here
cards.body: Some experts predict a machine able to break current encryption could appear within a decade, NIST said in 2024. It isn't waiting to find out. On August 13, 2024, NIST released its first three finalized encryption standards designed to withstand attack by a quantum computer, and urged organizations to start switching immediately. It plans to drop the vulnerable algorithms from its standards by 2035.

title: Hype and the Dot-Com Bubble
objective: After this level you can judge a new technology's hype using the rise and crash of internet stocks around 2000 as a guide.
summary: The Nasdaq peaked on March 10, 2000 and lost over three quarters by 2002; Pets.com lasted months. Yet 5.5 billion people were online by 2024. Split tech from price.

cards.headline: In 2000 the internet was the future. It was. The stocks weren't.
cards.body: Both halves of that sentence are true, and that's the lesson of the dot-com bubble. A technology can change the world while the money chasing it runs far ahead of reality.

cards.headline: The boom and the bust
cards.body: From 1995 the tech-heavy Nasdaq index rose quickly as money poured into internet start-ups, many overvalued and with little to show in the way of a product. That's a bubble: prices far above what the fundamentals justify, kept up by buyers hoping to sell to someone more optimistic. The Nasdaq peaked on March 10, 2000. By October 2002 it had lost more than three quarters of its value.

cards.headline: A sock puppet's short life
cards.body: Pets.com, famous for its sock-puppet mascot, became the era's symbol. It went public in February 2000 and shut down that November, having lost about $147 million since it started. By the end of 2001 most dot-com stocks, including Webvan and eToys, had gone bust. Some companies survived.

cards.headline: The technology kept going
cards.body: The crash hit share prices. It didn't unplug the internet: by 2024 about 5.5 billion people, 68% of the world, were online, the ITU estimates. So when a new technology is hyped, split the claim in two. Is the technology real? And is the price of betting on it sensible? The dot-com years answered yes, and no.

title: Is Moore's Law Over?
objective: After this level you can weigh the arguments over whether chip progress is slowing, and what engineers do now that shrinking is harder.
summary: Moore's law is a prediction, not physics. Clock rates stalled in the mid-2000s over power and heat, so chips added cores; now gains come from software, algorithms and specialized chips.

cards.headline: Is Moore's law dead? Two chip bosses gave opposite answers.
cards.body: In September 2022, Nvidia's chief executive said Moore's law was dead. Intel's chief executive said it was alive and well. Both run chip companies. So who's right? It depends on what you think the 'law' promises.

cards.headline: A prediction, not physics
cards.body: In 1965 Gordon Moore predicted that the number of transistors on a chip would double every year; in 1975 he revised it to every two years. That's an observation about an industry, not a law of nature like gravity. It set expectations for chipmakers and became a target they worked to meet. Nothing guarantees a target keeps being hit.

mascot.line: This connects to Level 8: the clock stopped speeding up, so chips found other ways to do more each second.

cards.headline: The speed that stopped
cards.body: Level 8's clock sets the pace of every step, and for years clock rates kept climbing. Then, in the mid-2000s, they stopped: extra speed was no longer worth the power it burned and the heat it made. So chipmakers split the work across several cores instead. Intel's rule of thumb: two cores at 80% of the clock rate give 73% more performance for the same power.

cards.headline: Where the gains come from now
cards.body: Transistors are nearing the limit of how small they can get, MIT researchers wrote in 2020. Future gains, they argued, must come from better software, smarter algorithms and hardware design, including chips customized for one job, which can be much more efficient. So 'Is Moore's law over?' has two honest halves: shrinking is getting harder, and computers can still get faster in other ways.

title: Open or Closed Software?
objective: After this level you can weigh the trade-offs between open-source and closed software for security, cost and control.
summary: Open-source code can be read, changed and shared by anyone; closed code stays secret. Log4j (2021) and Windows 10's 2025 end of support show each model's risks.

cards.headline: Some software lets anyone read its recipe. Some keeps it locked.
cards.body: Level 1 said software is the instructions that tell hardware what to do. Some makers publish those instructions for everyone; others keep them private. Which is safer, cheaper or better? It depends on what you're weighing.

cards.headline: What 'open' means
cards.body: Under the Open Source Definition, open-source software must come with its source code, the human-readable instructions, and its license must let anyone give it away or sell it, change it and share changed versions. Closed-source software publishes only the finished program and keeps its source code secret. Open doesn't have to mean free of charge. It means nobody can stop you reading, changing and passing it on.

cards.headline: Security: many eyes, few hands
cards.body: Anyone may inspect open code, and in November 2021 an outside security engineer reported a critical flaw in Log4j, open-source software used very broadly across services, websites and apps. It could let an attacker take control of a system. A US review board later found that projects like Log4j generally rely on volunteer teams without dedicated security resources. Open code gets many eyes; fixing it may rest on few hands.

cards.headline: Control: who decides when it ends?
cards.body: Closed software depends on its maker's choices. Windows 10 reached end of support on October 14, 2025: the PCs still work, but they no longer get security updates, apart from an extended program running to October 2027. With open code, anyone is allowed to keep maintaining a program. Each model trades one risk for another: who pays for the fixes, and who decides when they stop.

title: The Internet's Energy Bill
objective: After this level you can weigh estimates of how much electricity data centers use and what is driving the growth.
summary: Data centers used about 415 TWh in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity); the IEA projects about 945 TWh by 2030, driven by AI. Forecasts are ranges, so read them carefully.

cards.headline: How much electricity does the internet use? Depends who's counting, and when.
cards.body: Streaming, searching and AI all run in data centers, buildings packed with computers. Their electricity bill is real and growing. But the figures you read are estimates, and reading an estimate well is the skill.

cards.headline: Today's bill
cards.body: The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates data centers used about 415 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity in 2024, around 1.5% of the world's total. About 60% of a typical center's electricity powers the servers themselves. Cooling takes anywhere from about 7% in the most efficient giant centers to over 30% in less efficient ones. How a center is built changes its bill a lot.

cards.headline: Tomorrow's bill
cards.body: In its 2025 report, the IEA projects data-center use more than doubling to about 945 TWh by 2030, slightly more than all of Japan uses today, with AI the most important driver. For the US, a 2024 Berkeley Lab report found data centers used about 4.4% of the country's electricity in 2023, and set out scenarios of 6.7% to 12% by 2028.

cards.headline: Why the numbers disagree
cards.body: Look at that range again: the top of it is nearly double the bottom. That's because it's a set of scenarios, not a measurement. The data is patchy too: the US has no federal registration requirement for data centers, so even counts of how many exist vary by source. Read any energy figure like a scientist. Who made it, for which year, and is it counted or forecast?

title: Your Checklist for Tech Claims
objective: After this level you can run any claim about a gadget, app or AI through a short set of questions: how it works, who says so, and what it costs you.
summary: Three questions sort most tech claims: how does it work, who says so, what does it cost you. A VPN ad promising total anonymity fails all three.

cards.headline: 'Total anonymity online with one tap.' Should you believe it?
cards.body: This chapter has been practice for this moment. Three questions sort most tech claims: how does it work, who says so, and what does it cost you? Try them on a VPN ad.

cards.headline: 1. How does it work?
cards.body: A VPN routes your traffic through an encrypted tunnel to the VPN company's server. That hides it from your internet provider or the public Wi-Fi you're on. But your traffic comes out at the VPN's end, where the VPN provider can see it. So a VPN doesn't remove the watcher; it swaps one watcher for another. Knowing the mechanism already shrinks 'total anonymity' to 'a different company'.

cards.headline: 2. Who says so?
cards.body: The ad is written by the seller. Independent experts say something different: the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital-rights nonprofit, says a VPN is not a tool for anonymity, because companies have many other ways to track you. Give most weight to evidence from people with nothing to sell, like Level 92's researchers, who tested more than 17,000 apps instead of guessing.

mascot.line: Keep this: how does it work, who says so, what does it cost you? Three questions sort most claims.

cards.headline: 3. What does it cost you?
cards.body: Price isn't only money. Some free VPNs make their money by selling users' data, EFF warns, and the FTC advises checking whether a VPN app shares your information with third parties. A free tool you trust with all your traffic may cost more than a paid one. Ask what you hand over: money, data or trust.

learned: How does it work? A VPN moves trust, not removes it
Who says so? Prefer people with nothing to sell
